activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: The genetic code is read in codons of three bases; there are 64 possible codons but only 20 standard amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon.
story:
The codon chart was taped to the lab bench at an angle, and Alexa kept tilting her head to read it, as though the slant were the problem and not the chart itself. Their assignment was to build the full process out of paper cutouts: a strip of DNA, then a strip of mRNA, then a chain of folded paper amino acids, each one labeled with the three-base codon that called it into being. Ms. Çelik had left the room for the office, which meant twenty minutes of unsupervised assembly, and Chace was already folding his amino acids into paper airplanes.

"You're going to lose the pieces," Alexa said.

"I'm testing aerodynamics." He launched one; it clipped the fume hood and dropped behind the gas valve, unrecoverable. "Okay, that one's a glycine that has ascended."

Mattea, at the next bench, had arranged everything with terrible neatness: DNA template flat, mRNA laid parallel, a ruler marking the reading frame. Her want was simple and she had announced it on the first day of the unit, which was a slot at the regional biotech showcase in the spring, and she had decided that this paper model was the beginning of her portfolio. "If we get the sequence wrong, I'm redoing the whole thing," she said. "The judges will ask questions. They always ask questions."

Alexa returned to the chart. She had transcribed her DNA strip into mRNA, base by base, and now she was translating, running her pencil along the rows. CCG meant proline. She marked it. Then she hit CCC and looked it up and found proline again. She checked a third time, holding her finger flat against the paper so her eyes couldn't slide. Proline, still.

"That can't be right," she said aloud. "Two different codons, same amino acid?"

Chace leaned over, no longer entirely a dissident from the work, his curiosity finally bigger than his airplanes. "Maybe you read the row wrong."

"I didn't." But she kept going, and it kept happening. Leucine had not two but several codons pointing at it. Serine, the same. She began writing them in the margin of her handout, little clusters of three-letter codes collapsing into single amino acids, and the margin filled faster than she expected. Four bases, read three at a time, gave sixty-four possible codons; she counted the amino acid column and got twenty. Forty-four extra codons, most of them doubling or tripling up on the same twenty meanings. The code was not a one-to-one lock and key. It was more like a language with synonyms.

"Ms. Çelik would say there's a reason," Mattea said, squinting at Alexa's margin.

"She'd say there's a reason for everything, including why the third base matters less, probably." Alexa had heard Ms. Çelik's philosophy enough times to recite it: nature is conservative, nothing is wasted, look for the function. It was a way of thinking Alexa admired and half resisted, because it assumed the universe was tidy, and the chart in front of her looked less like tidiness than like something older and sloppier that had simply worked well enough to survive, the way the appendix was vestigial, a leftover that no one had gotten around to deleting.

When Ms. Çelik came back carrying a stack of photocopies, Alexa raised her hand before the teacher had even set them down. "The chart has repeats. CCG and CCC are both proline. Sixty-four codons, twenty amino acids. Is the chart wrong?"

Ms. Çelik smiled in a way that suggested the question had been planted in the assignment like a seed, though her expression also held genuine pleasure. "The chart is right. Codons are read three bases at a time," she said, and then she let the silence sit, hands folded, refusing to go further, which was her infuriating habit and probably her whole pedagogy.

"Fine," Alexa said. "I'll figure out the why myself."

"Good," said Ms. Çelik, and moved on to the next bench.

Alexa sat with it. Mattea, beside her, was ruminating out loud about whether the showcase judges would penalize a model that showed redundant codons, since it complicated the display, and Chace argued that the repeats were the interesting part, that a code with slack in it might be a code that could survive mistakes. Alexa found she wanted both of their positions to be true at once: the code as an elegant system, each piece necessary, and the code as something loose and forgiving, tolerant of error. She could not yet see how it was both. That it was both, she felt sure, the way the paper chain in front of her was both a model and a toy, both true and obviously not the thing itself.

"Write the synonyms in," she told Mattea. "Every codon, even the repeats. If the judges ask, tell them Alexa doesn't know why yet either."

Mattea clicked her pen twice, then printed CCC under CCG, both pointing to the same folded paper proline. "There," she said. "It's messy, but it's honest."

Chace retrieved a paper airplane from behind the gas valve, smoothed it flat on the bench, and wrote ALANINE on the wing.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Deliberate practice means working on specific weaknesses with a clear goal and immediate feedback, which improves skill more than simply playing through pieces already known.
story:
Layla had been playing the Chopin waltz for Mr. Fortin for eleven minutes when he raised one hand, palm out, and she stopped mid-phrase, the last note hanging in the warm air of the studio like a smell of rain.

"Again from the top," she said. "I almost had it that time."

"You had it the first four times," Mr. Fortin said. He was a wide, patient man who kept a metronome shaped like a pyramid and a kettle he never offered to anyone. "It's the same performance you gave me in September. It's lovely. It's finished. Close the book."

The audition for the youth orchestra was in five weeks, and the waltz was the one piece Layla could play all the way through without her hands shaking. The rest of the program sat in her folder like a debt: a sonata movement whose middle section she had been quietly skipping for two months, telling herself she'd fix it later. The two hard bars in particular, a stretch of fast broken chords where her fourth finger always collapsed, she had exhumed them only once, played them badly, and buried them again.

"Play me those two bars," Mr. Fortin said.

"Can I just do the waltz once more first?"

"No." He set his teacup down. "Two bars. Slowly. Then I'll tell you exactly what I hear, and you'll tell me what you're aiming for, and we'll go again. That's the whole hour."

She played the bars at half speed, and they were worse than she expected, graceless and lopsided, her weak finger slurring notes together like a drunk trying to walk a straight line. He stopped her at the fifth repetition. "Your wrist is high. Drop it." She dropped it. "Again." She went again, and again, and the tenth time through something small clicked, a cleannesse where there had been mush, and she felt a flash of something that was not exactly joy, more like the feeling of a door coming unlocked.

That night she texted Melodie, who had made the orchestra the year before without seeming to try. Layla wrote, Fortin made me play two bars for an hour. Worst hour of my life. Melodie's reply came fast: he did that to me too. it's called deliberate practice. Then a second message: i hated it. it's why i got in.

Layla sat on her bed with the phone warm in her hand. She had assumed Melodie was simply munificent with talent, the way some people seemed born having things, and it stung a little to learn that the ease had been built out of hours exactly like the one Layla had just survived. But it also rearranged something. If the gap between them was not nature but method, then the gap was closable, or at least narrrrowable, though she noticed she didn't fully believe that either. Plenty of people worked hard and still came in second. She couldn't tell yet which kind she was.

The next morning she arrived at the studio early, before her slot, and found the door ajar. Inside, Mr. Fortin was at the piano by himself, playing the same four measures over and over, stopping, frowning, going back. He was not performing anything. He was picking at something he couldn't do, like a neophyte, like her, his big hands clumsy on a passage she couldn't identify. She stood in the hallway with her folder against her chest, listening, deciding whether to knock.

When he finally noticed her, he didn't look embarrassed. He slid over on the bench and patted the seat beside him. "Two bars," he said. "Show me where we stopped."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Each transfer RNA carries one amino acid and has a three-base anticodon that pairs with the matching codon on the messenger RNA.
story:
The biology classroom smelled of potting soil because Mr. Chanthavong had expropriated the community garden's seedling tables for the afternoon, dragging them into the classroom until the custodian noticed. Each table held a strip of paper with three letters written on it: AUG, GGU, UAC, one after another in a line down the room. He handed out index cards and said only, "You are the ribosome. Feed yourselves." Then he sat by the window and drank his coffee as though the whole thing had nothing to do with him.

Camille held a card that read CCA on one side and, on the other, the word glycine. She turned it over twice. Around her, Calla was already voluble, narrating her own card to anyone within earshot: proline, hers said, with the letters GGU, and she seemed to find this personally flattering. Marwa stood at the start of the line with the card that said UAC, which she had not stopped staring at since she got it.

"I don't get what I'm supposed to do with this," Marwa said.

"You match," Camille said, though she wasn't sure of it yet. She walked the line of tables, reading the codons aloud, and noticed that each card in the room carried exactly one amino acid, never two, never none. Each card also had one three-letter code. She stopped at the first table, AUG, and watched a boy lay his card beside it, letters to letters.

In middle school Camille had played the violin badly for two years, and what she remembered most was the moment the teacher stopped correcting her and simply played the phrase himself, once, and let her steal it by ear. It had felt less like being taught than like being caught doing something she already knew. She had that feeling again now, standing over the seedling tables, except here there was no one to copy from. Mr. Chanthavong was on his second coffee and visibly committed to saying nothing.

"The letters pair up," Marwa said suddenly, from her table. "A with U. So UAC on my card goes with AUG on the table." She set her card down, and it fit, C to G, A to U, U to A, letter for letter backwards. "So the card is like, a opposite of the table."

"An anticodon," Calla said, reading her own card upside down. "It says anticodon right here, Camille, in the corner. In very small print." She held it out as evidence, as though this settled a court case.

Camille took the card from her and turned it the right way up. Calla's card carried proline and the anticodon GGU, and the table it matched carried CCA. She checked Marwa's, then the boy's, then her own: CCA on her card, glycine, and the table marked GGU. Every card in the room carried one amino acid and one three-base anticodon, and every anticodon paired with its codon on the line of tables, letter against letter, all the way down.

Then the problem arrived, because the line of tables ran out. The last codon was UAA, and no one's card matched it. Marwa, who had been moving down the line with growing confidence, stood at the end holding a card that would not fit anywhere and looked, briefly, like a person whose bus had pulled away. She had wanted, Camille realized, to finish it. She had wanted to walk the whole line and hand off every amino acid and see the thing completed, and now the paper strip just stopped.

"Maybe that's the point," Camille said. "Maybe the line ending is part of it."

Mr. Chanthavong lowered his coffee cup an inch, which for him was practically applause. Marwa frowned at the empty space past the last table, then set her card down anyway, in the air past the end, and let go of it. It fluttered to the floor and lay there, face up, amino acid side showing.

"That's my glycine," Camille said, picking up her own card again, "or it's nobody's now. I genuinely can't tell you which."

"Then let's do it again," Marwa said, "and this time I want the stop codon."

"How do you know it's called that?" Calla asked.

"I read the whole chapter last night," Marwa said. "Twice. Some of us prepare."

Camille lined her card up against the second table, CCA against GGU, and waited for Marwa to come hand her the next one.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: To find customers with no orders, a common SQL pattern LEFT JOINs customers to orders and keeps only rows where the orders' customer ID IS NULL.
story:
The bell over the door of Sato Phone Repair had not rung in forty minutes, and Alexandre was grateful, because the spreadsheet open on the shop's ancient laptop was refusing to cooperate. Mr. Sato had gone to the back to solder a charging port, leaving Alexandre with the customer list and the order history in two separate files, and a question that had seemed simple at nine that morning: which customers have never ordered anything? His mother had asked it over dinner two nights ago, half-joking about the shop she kept accounts for, and Alexandre had said, too quickly, that it would take him ten minutes. That had been a small vanity, and he knew it now.

He had started by hand. Cross out every name that appeared in the orders file, keep the ones that did not. Twenty customers in, with a hundred and sixty to go, he understood that the two files were really two tables, and that somewhere in what he'd read online last winter there was a way to make the software do the crossing out for him. He typed a query, ran it, and got an error about a missing expression, which told him only that he had guessed at the syntax.

"You look like a man arguing with a vending machine," Mikaela said from the doorway, shaking rain off her jacket. She had texted that morning: brought your charger, the one you left at Marc-Antoine's, and since I am a generous person I expect payment in gossip. Alexandre had answered with a single line, come by Sato's, I'm losing to a database, and she had come.

He showed her the screen anyway. Two tables, customers and orders, each order carrying the customer's ID. "I want the ones who ordered nothing," he said. "The opposite of a match." Mikaela leaned in, chewing the end of her pen the way she did in exams, and said she remembered something from her brother's notes, something about joins. A join, as far as either of them could reconstruct it, matched rows from one table to rows in another. That found the customers who had ordered. It found the opposite of what he wanted.

It was Mr. Sato, coming out front to test the repaired phone, who ruined the guesswork by handing Alexandre a yellowed textbook from under the counter. "From my night course," he said. "Before this place was mine and I stopped being anybody's student." He did not stay to teach it; he sat by the window with the phone and a charging cable, and left Alexandre to the pages.

There it was, in a chapter with diagrams like railway switches. An inner join kept only the matched rows. A left join kept every row from the first table, matched or not, and where no match existed, the columns from the second table came back empty, marked NULL. Alexandre read the sentence twice, then a third time, because the consequence arrived slowly. If you left joined customers to orders, every customer survived, matched or unmatched, and the unmatched ones were exactly the ones whose order columns were empty. You did not search for absence directly. You built a table where absence left a mark, then kept only the marked rows.

He typed it out, hands slightly unsteady, saying it under his breath to fix it in memory: "Left join customers to orders, then keep only the rows where the orders' customer ID is null." Mikaela watched the screen. He ran it. Fourteen rows. Not a guess, not a crossed-out list, but fourteen names, each of them someone who had walked in or called once and never come back. He recognized one, a woman who had eulogized her dead flip phone at the counter in June, so tenderly that Mr. Sato had promised to bury it in the drawer of unclaimed devices rather than recycle it. She had never ordered a replacement.

Marc-Antoine would have called the drawer of dead phones a museum of speciation, every model drifting further from its ancestors, and Alexandre could almost hear him being facetious about it, holding up a slider phone and naming it a missing link. He caught himself smiling, then stopped, because the fourteen names had changed something for him and he was not sure yet what. He had told his mother it would take ten minutes because showing off had felt better than saying I don't know, teach me. Two days later, with a borrowed textbook and a friend's half-memory and a quiet man at the window who had once been a student too, he had the answer, and it had cost exactly the honesty he had skipped at dinner.

"Text her the list?" Mikaela asked.

"In a minute." He copied the fourteen names into a message to his mother, typed I was wrong, it took longer than I said, and read it over once before deciding whether that sentence could stand. Outside, the rain thickened against the glass, and Mr. Sato plugged the repaired phone into its charger and watched the screen light up.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier.
story:
The first loaf had come out of the oven like a brick with ambitions, dense in the middle and crumbly at the edges, and Sophie had stood over the cooling rack for a long minute before she said anything to anyone. Her mother had praised it anyway, sawing at it with the good knife, buttering each ragged slice as though raggedness were a style. Sophie, seventeen and unwilling to accept butter as a solution, had gone to bed with the taste of failure still floury at the back of her teeth.

Now it was Saturday again, and she had the kitchen to herself. Her mother was at the market, her younger brother at his practice, and the counter was dusted white under the window light. She measured the flour into the big ceramic bowl the way the recipe said, leveled the cup with the back of a knife, added the yeast to warm water and watched it bloom, faintly beery, before she stirred it in.

She had texted Kane the night before, because Kane had baked bread all last winter. He showed up at the door with his sleeves already pushed up, holding his phone like evidence.

"Okay, so I looked it up," he said, setting the phone on the counter between the salt and the sugar. "It's the kneading. That's the whole thing. Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water."

"Which are what?"

"Wheat proteins, that's all I know. But here's the part that matters. Kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger, and the bread chewier. Your loaf was dense and crumbly, so either you barely kneaded it, or something else went sideways."

Sophie turned the shaggy dough out onto the counter. "I kneaded it. I think. For a while."

"For how long?"

She had to admit she didn't know. She had kneaded it until she felt bored, which last Saturday had meant about three minutes. The recipe said eight to ten. She had read that line and decided the writer was being cautious, the way recipes were cautious about everything, and she had litigated the point silently, in her own head, and ruled in her own favor. The evidence had since been eaten, buttered, every crumb.

"Start counting," Kane said. "I'll time you."

The first minutes were nothing much. She pressed with the heel of her hand, folded, turned, pressed again, and the dough stayed sticky and reluctant, clinging to her knuckles. Around minute five something shifted under her palms, subtle, almost seismic in the small world of the counter: the dough began to push back. It smoothed. It stretched when she pulled it and held, faintly translucent at the thinnest point, like something that had decided to trust her.

"That's it," Kane said, leaning in. "That's the window thing. You can see light through it."

"That's the gluten?"

"That's the gluten network, I think. Stronger now. You made that happen."

It was a strange thought, that her boredom had been the variable, that the difference between brick and bread had been five extra minutes of her hands doing the same patient thing. She kept kneading past the timer because it felt good now, warm and responsive under her palms, and she let it rest in the oiled bowl and watched it swell, slow as a tide, filling the bowl's shadowed curve.

Ms. Bennett, the neighbor from across the back fence, appeared at the door around noon with a carton of eggs she was distributing among the street. She smelled the bread before she saw it. "Oh, that takes me back," she said. "My mother's kitchen on a cold day. Is it your first?"

"Second," Sophie said. "The first one was a doorstop."

"Everyone's first is a doorstop." Ms. Bennett looked into the bowl at the risen dough, pillowed and soft, and did not offer advice, which Sophie appreciated more than she could have said. She only took her eggs and left, waving through the window as she crossed the yard.

The loaf went into the hot oven and Sophie sat on the floor in front of the glass door, watching it, a low hum of foreboding under her ribs that she couldn't entirely dismiss. Maybe the yeast was old. Maybe the water had been too warm. There were variables she couldn't see, and she understood that she was betting on only one of them. Kane sat on the counter with his phone, not looking at it, both of them quiet while the smell filled the room, toasted and sweet and wheaty.

When she knocked on the bottom of the cooled loaf and heard the hollow sound the recipe had promised, she carried it to the counter, took the good knife, and cut the first slice while Kane leaned over her shoulder. The crumb tore open even and soft, and she held a piece up to the window to see the light through it.

"Chewy," she said, testing it, and handed him the knife.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections.
story:
David had been chosen, he suspected, because he was the only one who volunteered, and he was the only one who volunteered because the poster had mentioned an honorarium, a word he had to look up and which turned out to mean a polite sum of money that made the whole thing sound more dignified than it was. Forty dollars to stand in front of a ninth-grade health class and explain consent, contraception, and how to get tested at the clinic on Fairmount Avenue. Mr. Qureshi, who ran the peer educator program, had shaken his hand and said, "You'll do a teach-back for me Thursday. If you can teach it to me, you can teach it to anyone."

The problem was that David did not know it yet himself, not really, not in the way that survives questions. He knew the words. He could recite the definition of consent like a pledge, enthusiastic, ongoing, reversible. But when his little cousin had asked him at dinner why people couldn't just say yes once and have it count forever, David had opened his mouth and produced a sentence with three clauses and no verbs that mattered.

So he took to the bathroom. It was the only room with a lock and a mirror, and the mirror was the only audience that wouldn't prevaricate about his performance out of politeness. He stood at the sink with his notes folded in his back pocket and addressed his reflection. "Consent," he told the mirror, "is like a green light. It means go, but you still watch the road." He grimaced. His reflection grimaced back with perfect sincerity, which was somehow worse. He tried again. "Okay, imagine you lend someone your bike." He paused. "Can you ask for the bike back?" The reflection waited, and David thought of his cousin, and thought of Tamara, and thought that a bike was a bad metaphor because nobody ever felt heartbroken about a bike, and anyway that was the point, that the ninth graders would already know this from their lives, and his job was not to give them the feeling but the words for it.

He was on his fourth draft of the bike metaphor when Tamara texted him. Emerson says you're doing the sex talk. Did you know Emerson calls it the sex talk. Also I need to go to the pharmacy, come with me, I refuse to sit in the waiting area alone while they judge me.

The pharmacy was four blocks from school. Tamara walked fast when she was embarrassed, and by the time they reached the automatic doors she had outlined her entire position on the situation: she had a prescription for birth control, her mother knew, everything was fine and boring, but she hated the pickup counter because the pharmacist always looked at her like she was a math problem. "You're the peer educator," she said. "You stand next to me and absorb the judgment."

The pharmacist, a small woman with reading glasses on a chain, did not in fact look at Tamara like a math problem. She looked at the prescription, typed, and slid a white paper bag across the counter. Tamara, gathering her courage in both hands, asked the question she'd apparently been carrying for a week. "Does it, um. Does this protect against infections too?" The pharmacist said, "No, it doesn't do anything for infections. Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces that risk." Then she said, "Anything else, hon," and turned to the printer.

David stood very still, as though the sentence were a butterfly he might frighten off. He had spent two evenings in the bathroom learning to say the word contraception without tripping over it, and in eight seconds at a pickup counter he had learned something his notes had buried in a footnote he'd never read past. The pill prevented pregnancy. It did nothing about infections. Condoms, alone among the common methods, did both. He heard it in the pharmacist's tired, flat voice, the voice of someone who said it forty times a week, and it landed differently than any footnote ever had.

Outside, Emerson was leaning against the bike rack, looking saturnine in the way he did when he wanted to be asked what was wrong. "What's wrong," David said. "Tamara got her prescription and I learned the single most important fact I've ever learned," David said, "and you're doing your face."

"I'm doing my face because you two are going to stand up in front of children and talk about this, and I have to sit in the audience knowing all of you." Emerson pulled his hood up. "Also the clinic thing. You're really going to tell them how to get tested?"

"That's the job," David said. Tamara held up her paper bag like evidence. "You walk in, you don't need a parent, you can call ahead, and it's free or cheap," she recited, in the flat voice of someone quoting David's notes back at him, which was how he learned she'd actually read them. "He made me quiz him. Twice."

On Thursday, Mr. Qureshi sat in the last desk of the empty classroom with his arms crossed, and David stood at the whiteboard and discovered his hands wanted to be in his pockets and his voice wanted to be an octave lower, and he let neither of them win. He talked about consent with the bike metaphor, revised, and Mr. Qureshi said, "Good, but what if they ask about pressure? What if someone says it ruins the mood?" David said, "Then I say the mood is not a person's whole life, and also that asking is not that hard, people do harder things every day, like parallel parking." Mr. Qureshi's mouth twitched.

When David got to contraception, he drew a line down the whiteboard. "Pill prevents pregnancy," he said. "Doesn't touch infections. Condoms are the only common method that does both." He said it the way the pharmacist had said it, plain, no drama, and then he kept going to the clinic part, the phone number, the walk-in hours, the part where nobody's parents were called. Mr. Qureshi uncrossed his arms and wrote something on his clipboard. "One more question," he said. "What if a kid asks you something you don't know?"

"Then I say I don't know," David said, "and I find out, and I tell them Monday." He capped the marker. In the doorway, Tamara gave him a thumbs up, and behind her Emerson held up a torn piece of notebook paper that said, in enormous letters, PARALLEL PARKING.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: One mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere of pressure.
story:
Gabrielle had taped the balloon to the top of the display board so it hung above her title, and by nine in the morning it had already begun to sag, which she took as a kind of commentary on the whole enterprise. The title read HOW BIG IS A MOLE? in letters she had traced and retraced until they looked confident. Behind her, Dion was trying to get the folding table to stop rocking with a folded square of paper towel, and Kiara was arranging the jars of sugar, salt, and iron filings in what she insisted was a visually pleasing gradient.

"You're sure about the number?" Dion asked. He wasn't being difficult. He was the sort of person who checked things twice and then apologized for checking them.

"Twenty-two point four litres," Gabrielle said. "At zero degrees Celsius and one atmosphere. For an ideal gas, one mole of it takes up that much space. That's the whole point of the box."

The box sat at the centre of the table, a cardboard cube she had measured and cut in her grandmother's garage in February, when the project was still an idea and not yet an encumbrance she carried on the bus every morning. Its sides were a little over twenty-eight centimetres each, which made it just about twenty-two point four litres, give or take the sloppiness of her knife work. She had painted the edges white and written ONE MOLE OF IDEAL GAS on the front in the same confident letters.

The trouble was the calculation beside it. Her chemistry teacher, Ms. Do, had suggested the demonstration last month, and Gabrielle had said yes before she fully understood what she was agreeing to, which was to work backward from a mass of reactant to moles of product, and then forward from moles to volume. She had a paragraph on the board explaining it, and under the paragraph, her worked example, and in the worked example, she was no longer sure she had divided where she should have multiplied.

She remembered the night she built the box. Her grandmother had come out to the garage in her housecoat to ask what the noise was, and when Gabrielle explained, holding the cardboard sides up like walls of a tiny house, her grandmother had stood there a long moment and then said, "So you're telling me that much air weighs as much as a small bag of potatoes." She meant a mole of an ideal gas at those cold, ordinary conditions, and she had it nearly right, and Gabrielle had been so pleased that someone outside the classroom understood what she was doing that she had not checked her arithmetic until eleven that night, and then again at midnight, with different answers each time.

"Gabrielle." Kiara touched her elbow. "Judges. Row three. The one with the lanyard keeps looking over here."

The gym smelled of floor wax and someone else's vinegar-and-baking-soda volcano, which had already erupted once and been mopped up by a custodian with heroic patience. Ms. Do moved along the aisle with a clipboard, pausing at each table, and Gabrielle understood that she would come here too, and that she would look at the paragraph and the worked example, and that she would see the place where the numbers turned.

The first judge arrived alone, a woman with reading glasses on a chain. She asked what the box was for. Gabrielle turned it in her hands and said, "If you had exactly one mole of an ideal gas, at zero degrees Celsius and one atmosphere of pressure, it would fill this. Twenty-two point four litres. That's the space it takes up." The judge nodded slowly and wrote something down.

"And this?" She tapped the paragraph.

"That's the part I'm working on," Gabrielle said. She could have demurred, could have slid the conversation back toward the balloon and the jars, but she heard herself keep going. "I start with a mass of reactant, I convert to moles using its molar mass, then I use the reaction to find the moles of product. The problem is my example. I did it twice at home and got two different volumes, and I brought both, because I honestly don't know which one is right."

The judge looked at her over the glasses. "You brought both."

"It felt dishonest to hide one."

When the judge moved on, Dion leaned in. "Which one do you believe?"

"The smaller one. I think I converted grams to moles right that time. Molar mass on the bottom, so the grams cancel. In the other one I flipped it, and the moles came out too small, and then the volume came out too small, and I didn't notice because the answer still looked plausible." She said it quietly, and found that saying it out loud made it truer, or at least harder to un-know.

Ms. Do arrived during the mid-morning lull, when the volcano at the far end was being refilled and Kiara had gone to find the washroom. She read the board from top to bottom without touching it, then set her clipboard against her hip.

"The box is good," she said. "Where did you get the dimensions?"

"I calculated the volume and took the cube root. Twenty-two point four litres, so the sides come out to about twenty-eight point two centimetres." Gabrielle waited. "The stoichiometry paragraph is the part I'm unsure about. I put my putative answer on the left and the other one on the right, and I labelled them, but I didn't pick one."

Ms. Do looked at the two columns for a moment. "Which is the one you'd defend if you had to?"

"The left. Grams of reactant, divided by molar mass, gives moles. Then the ratio from the equation gives moles of product. Then moles times twenty-two point four gives litres at those conditions." She pointed at each step as she said it, and her finger did not shake, though her voice came out smaller than she intended.

Ms. Do nodded once and moved toward Dion's end of the table, and did not say whether it was right, which Gabrielle understood was its own kind of answer, or possibly no answer at all.

By noon the balloon had sagged almost to the title. Kiara came back with two juice boxes and handed one to Gabrielle, who set it down beside the box, took the marker from the tray, and crossed out the right-hand column with a single unhurried line.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open.
story:
The letter from Hollis College was two sentences long, and Alexandra had read it enough times to have burnished it smooth in her mind: the committee was pleased to offer her a place on the waitlist, decisions would follow as space permitted, thank you for your patience. Her mother kept saying it was practically an acceptance, which was a way of saying it wasn't one. It was April seventeenth, and the kitchen table between them was covered with the machinery of the decision: the deposit slip for Alderman University, the checkbook, a mug of tea gone cold, and her laptop open to a forum thread titled WAITLIST 2025 where a hundred strangers reported their outcomes like weather.

"May first is the deadline everywhere," her mother said, tapping the deposit slip. "Alderman wants an answer and five hundred dollars."

"I know when it is, Mom."

"You could put the deposit down and still get off the waitlist at Hollis. That happens."

Alexandra didn't answer, because the answer was complicated, and her mother wanted it simple. What she had learned, from the forum and from reading the admissions blogs of eleven colleges over three nights, was this: many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open. Which meant the waitlist wasn't a queue she was standing in. It was a warehouse of spare parts, and the college wouldn't even count its openings until after everyone like her had paid somewhere else.

Jillian came over that evening, which she did most Tuesdays, ostensibly to study for the AP Lit exam and actually to eat Alexandra's family's better snacks. She wanted the last of the peanut butter pretzels and, less openly, she wanted to talk about the dorms at Bexley, where she'd gotten in early and where Alexandra had not applied at all. Tonight she was voluble about roommate questionnaires, having filled hers out in what she described as a spirit of radical honesty. "I said I go to bed at two and I'm messy," she announced, wiping pretzel salt on her jeans. "They can't say I didn't warn them."

"I have to decide about the deposit," Alexandra said.

"Then decide. Alderman's fine. You said the physics program was fine."

"Fine," Alexandra said, in a tone that made Jillian look up.

They had reached a kind of detente on the subject of colleges months ago, an unspoken agreement that Jillian would stop narrating Bexley's dining hall and Alexandra would stop performing indifference. The pretzel bag crinkled. Down the hall the dryer buzzed and nobody moved.

"Here's the thing," Alexandra said, and turned the laptop so Jillian could see the thread. "The deposits are due May first. Everybody sends them, that's how the whole system works. Then the college counts its empty seats. Then, in May, if they're short, they go to the waitlist. So the money I'd send Alderman is the thing that tells Hollis whether there's even a spot."

"That's deranged."

"It's arithmetic."

"It's deranged arithmetic. You'd be paying five hundred dollars to help the college that rejected you do its math."

Alexandra laughed, which she hadn't done about the letter yet. Her mother drifted through in her slippers, refilled her own mug without asking, and said, "Jessica's mother told me you should write to the dean. A letter. To burnish your file. She said that word, burnish."

"She did say that word," Alexandra admitted, after her mother had gone. "Jessica sent one. Two pages, single-spaced."

"You're not sending two pages."

"I sent a paragraph. Tuesday. I said Hollis was still my first choice and I'd take a spot in the spring if they had one." She said it lightly, the way you report something that no longer belongs to you.

Mr. Whitaker, who had retired next door and who was, in his own estimation, the street's standing authority on all applications, encountered her at the mailbox on Wednesday and asked after the verdict. When she said waitlist, he nodded slowly and said that in his day you'd drive up and shake a hand, and she thanked him and carried the mail inside, where she sat back down at the table and did what she had been circling for a week.

She filled out the Alderman deposit slip in her careful handwriting. Then she wrote the date she would stop checking the forum, June first, on a sticky note, and stuck it to the laptop lid where she would see it every morning. It wasn't surrender and it wasn't hope; it was more like hedging a bet she had already lost once and might lose again, and she was honest enough with herself to admit she couldn't tell which one the five hundred dollars was buying. Her mother came in, saw the slip, and put a hand briefly on Alexandra's shoulder on her way to the sink.

At dinner they ate in ordinary silence, forks and the hum of the refrigerator. Alexandra's phone sat face-down beside her plate. When it buzzed against the wood she turned it over, read the screen, and set it down again without saying anything. Jillian, on the front step later, asked what it had been.

"The portal," Alexandra said. "Just the portal updating. It does that."

"Does it?"

"They'll send an email if it's anything. An email is anything." She looked at the dark shape of the Whitakers' porch light across the hedge, then closed the phone in her fist like a coin she hadn't decided how to spend.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Signalling before a merge or lane change warns other drivers of the move; signalling too late, or not at all, gives them no time to adjust.
story:
Grayson set his keys on the kitchen table, beside the folded note from Ms. Whitaker, his neighbour two doors down, who had agreed to supervise his practice hours because his mother worked nights and his father no longer drove at all. The note was written on the back of a grocery receipt in her small, upright hand. "Saturday, nine sharp. We will do the highway merge first, then parking behind the church on Delmore. Bring your glasses. And thank you for the tomatoes, which were perfect." He read it twice, then folded it again along its old crease, wondering whether the precision of the order of operations was kindness or a verdict on how far behind he was. The road test was in eleven days and he had never once merged at speed.

He had a theory about that, which he'd been litigating with himself all week: that driving was basically applied rationalism, a system of rules that rewarded you for thinking clearly and punished you for hesitating. His father used to say something like that, back when he still drove, back before the thing with his eyes. Rules, his father said, are what you have instead of luck. Rosaly, who had passed her own test in February, disagreed over text while Grayson sat at the kitchen counter eating cereal for dinner.

her message had said, in three bubbles sent during her shift at the garden centre: "its not rules its ppl. every1 in a car is guessing what the others will do. the rules are just how u guess out loud." He had typed and deleted three replies before settling on "that's bleak," and she had answered with a thumbs-up, which told him nothing.

Saturday came cold and bright. Ms. Whitaker drove them to the on-ramp in her grey sedan and then made him switch seats, folding herself into the passenger side with her coffee still steaming in a travel mug she'd brought from her own kitchen, as though the whole enterprise were domestic, an errand. He accelerated up the ramp, checked the mirror, and flicked the signal on at the same moment he began to move the wheel toward the gap in traffic. A horn sounded behind them, long and personal.

"Signal first," Ms. Whitaker said, not raising her voice. "Before, not during. Signalling before a merge warns other drivers of the move. Too late, or not at all, and they've got no time to adjust." She sipped her coffee. "Try it again at the next loop."

They circled the industrial park and came back to the ramp. This time he pressed the lever early, three seconds before he intended to move, and watched the mirror. The car that had been sitting in his blind spot, a white pickup with a ladder rack, eased back, headlights lifting as the driver touched the brake. The gap opened the way a door opens, deliberately, because someone on the other side had been told he was coming. He slid into the lane and his hands were shaking and Ms. Whitaker said nothing at all, which he understood as the highest grade she awarded.

Behind the church on Delmore, between two orange cones she had set out herself, he parallel parked on the fourth attempt. He kept clipping the rear cone, overcorrecting, and she finally got out, moved the cone to the exact curb position, and stood in the cold with her arms crossed, saying only "slower" each time he reversed. On the fourth try the tyres found the kerb with a soft kiss and she nodded once, a small subterranean tremor of approval passing across her face and gone. He sat in the idling car afterward, hands on the wheel, and thought about the pickup driver. The man had done something for a stranger, eased off for no reason except a blinking light, and Grayson realized Rosaly had been describing the same system his father had, from the other side. His father's rules and Rosaly's guessing-out-loud were one thing: the signal was the rule, and the rule was a way of telling the truth in advance.

He was less sure what to do with the part that stayed uncertain. The horn on the first merge had been aimed at him, and it had been deserved, and the second merge had gone smoothly, but he couldn't claim the second driver's kindness was guaranteed by anything. The signal warned people; it didn't compel them. Somewhere out there a driver would see the blinker and speed up to close the gap, because a rule told in advance could still be answered with refusal.

That afternoon, back in his own kitchen, his mother asleep after her shift, he texted Rosaly: "you were right. its both." She replied with a voice memo, thirty seconds of her laughing in the greenhouse wind. "Monday I'll follow you on the highway and we'll merge like a funeral procession. Very dignified." Then, from Ms. Whitaker, a second note in his mother's mailbox, another receipt on the back: "Tuesday, same time. You are less terrible than you believe. The cones will be exactly where I left them." Grayson put both notes in the drawer with the takeaway menus, set his keys on top of them, and stood looking out the kitchen window at the empty street where he would practise pulling out in the morning.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: India has marked voters' fingers with indelible ink based on silver nitrate since its 1962 general election, so no one can vote twice.
story:
The line at the community hall stretched past the folding tables and out toward the coat rack, and Eric stood in it holding his registration card so tightly that the edges curled. Behind him, Taylor was arguing with Rami about whether a single vote mattered in a district that had gone the same way for thirty years. "It's symbolic," Taylor said. "Symbols are fine, but they don't fix the pothole on Marsh Street." Rami said something about how everything was symbolic if you were lazy about it, and then they both looked at Eric, who was eighteen as of March and had spent the whole drive here not saying which way he was going to vote, partly because his father had told him over dinner that politicians were uniformly crooked and his mother had said, with unusual heat, that saying that was a way of excusing yourself from trying.

At the check-in table, a woman with a clipboard found his name and asked for ID. While she copied his details, Eric noticed an old photograph taped to the front of the table, beside the "VOTE TODAY" sign the scouts had made. It showed a man, his mother's cousin, holding up his right hand for the camera, and the finger nearest his thumb was stained a deep purple-black, as if he had dipped it in ink and let it dry there. A little girl beside Eric, waiting with her mother, pointed at it. "Why is his finger dirty?"

"That's not dirt," the woman at the table said without looking up. "That's from voting in India. They mark your finger with indelible ink made with silver nitrate, and they've done it that way since their 1962 general election, so no one can vote twice."

"Even if you wash it?" the girl asked.

"Even if you wash it," the woman said, and stamped something on Eric's card and waved him toward the booths.

Taylor peered at the photograph as they shuffled forward. "My uncle says stuff like that doesn't work here, that we should need it, because of all the fraud." Rami said his social studies teacher had put a number on fraud by impersonation at the polls, and the number was so small Taylor laughed at it, scathing, the way he laughed at anything that disagreed with him. "Fine," Taylor said. "Then it's about probity, isn't it. Trust. You mark everyone because you trust no one, or you mark no one because you trust everyone." Eric said that didn't sound like trust, it sounded like a receipt. Nobody marks you to insult you. They mark you so the mark can vouch for you.

His mother's cousin's name, he remembered, was one his grandmother always refused to transliterate into English letters, saying the sound didn't survive the trip, and so the family wrote it two ways and the second way was never right. He had been thinking about that all week, about how the same thing could be said twice and come out different each time, and how his father and his mother were both talking about the same country with entirely different mouths.

The booth was smaller than he expected. The pencil was tied to the shelf with a string too short to write comfortably, and he had to hunch. He looked at the ballot and found that he did not know some of the names, and for one office he genuinely could not remember what he had read about either candidate, and he sat there long enough that the man behind him coughed. He thought about his father saying all politicians lie, which was easy to say and impossible to act on, because refusing to choose was still a choice, just an unlabeled one. He thought about the ink on his cousin's finger, which stayed whether you were proud of it or not.

He filled in the rest and left the one office blank. It was the honest thing and it felt like less than nothing.

Outside the booth, an older volunteer tore his ballot stub and handed it back, and Taylor was already at the folding table where Ms. Wanjiru, who had taught him chemistry two years ago and now ran the polling station, was taking down the sign at the coffee urn. "Well?" she said. "You look like a man who's had an argument with himself."

"I left one blank," Eric said.

"Then you voted better than most people," she said, and stacked the cups.

Rami was waiting by the door, and Taylor was holding it open, and the three of them walked out into the parking lot where the light was going flat and amber over the cars. "So which way?" Taylor asked, and Eric got into the back seat and pulled the door shut.

"Drive," he said.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria, and splits one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules for a net gain of two ATP.
story:
The pond behind the school had one good bench, and Charles had claimed it with his biology notes spread across the slats like a hand of cards he kept losing. The unit test was Monday. Somewhere in his diagram of the cell, drawn three times and erased twice, the whole process had stopped making sense, and he had walked out here with the last of the afternoon because the library felt like a place where things had already been decided.

"You're drawing a mitochondrion with a smile," said Frederique, dropping onto the far end of the bench and shaking water off her sleeves. She had been skipping stones. The pond accepted them without comment.

"It's the outer membrane. And it's a frown, technically." He held the page up. Inside the blob he had written the whole story of glucose, arrows marching from left to right, every step tucked inside the organelle where he assumed it belonged. ATP at the end, like a trophy.

Frederique leaned over. She was the sort of person who read other people's notes the way other people read horoscopes, half-critical and half-fascinated. "Why is glycolysis in there?"

"That's where respiration happens. Mitochondria. It's the whole point of them."

"Is it, though." She said it flat, not a question, and picked up a flat stone and turned it over in her fingers, judicious about which face would meet the water. "Dana quizzed me on the walk over. She's already memorized it and she's insufferable about it."

Charles looked at his arrows. Somewhere in the reading there had been a phrase, and he had filed it under details and moved on, the way he filed anything that complicated a diagram he'd already committed to. He flipped back two pages in his notes. There it was, in his own handwriting, because he copied everything the board said whether he understood it or not: the first step happened before the mitochondria, out in the cytoplasm, in the open soup of the cell. Glycolysis happened there, and it split one glucose into two pyruvate molecules. Two ATP out of the deal. Net gain, the notes said, as though the cell were a small business.

"So the first step doesn't even happen in there," he said. He felt oddly betrayed by his own drawing, which he had spent an hour decorating with detail that was, in this one respect, a lie.

"What's the net gain again?" Frederique asked, still weighing the stone.

"Two ATP. For one glucose. Two pyruvate going forward." He said it and heard how it sounded like a recipe, and how a recipe was maybe what it was: what the cell does with sugar when it wants to keep moving. Skipping stones was the same kind of thing, he thought, a small transaction of energy, muscle spending what the mitochondria had banked. He didn't say that aloud, because he had eulogized enough dead metaphors in class essays to know when a teacher would write "stretch" in the margin.

He took out a fresh page and began again. This time he drew the cell first, whole, and put glycolysis out in the cytoplasm where it belonged, a small crowded step before the big machine took over. The mitochondria got the rest, the arrows converging on it like people toward a lit doorway. It was less tidy than his first version. The truth of it seemed to be that the cell did its business in stages, in different rooms, and the elegance he'd imagined, one organelle doing everything, was an elegance he had invented because it drew well.

"Volition," Frederique said suddenly.

"What?"

"Your word list. It's due Monday too, isn't it." She grinned and skipped her stone. It went once, twice, sank on the third. "You're welcome."

"Nobody asked you to tutor me in vocabulary."

"Nobody asked me to tutor you in cells either, and yet." She stood, dusting off her knees, and pointed at his new diagram. "Is that right now?"

Charles looked at it. He thought it was. He thought the cytoplasm was right, and the split, and the count of two, and he could recite all of it by morning. What he couldn't yet see was why the cell would run its first step outside the power plant, what advantage there was in doing the opening move in open ground, and the book had not said and Frederique certainly didn't know. That part he would carry around unsolved, the way he carried most interesting things.

"Dana's going to ask you the net gain," Frederique said, backing away down the slope toward the water. "Tell her two, and don't give her the satisfaction of hesitating."

"Two," Charles said, to the pond, to the diagram, to the small wrong frown he was about to erase.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Melvyn Leffler's A Preponderance of Power, which won the 1993 Bancroft Prize, argued US leaders pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world.
story:
The museum's Cold War gallery smelled of dust and floor wax, and Maelle had been standing in front of the same glass case for eleven minutes. Inside it sat a fallout shelter poster, a ration booklet, and a school desk from 1962 with a laminated card of instructions tucked into the desktop. Her essay was due Monday, and Mr. Perera had written one comment across the top of her draft: "You have Gaddis's view. Where is the counterview? Evidence, not vibes."

"I don't even know what a counterview would look like," she said. Callie leaned against the case beside her, unwrelling a granola bar despite the NO FOOD sign.

"It would look like a book," Callie said. "Books have views. That's kind of their thing."

Rohan came over from the Korea exhibit with his phone out, showing a photo of a rationed beef label. "I asked the docent guy for you. The one with the lanyard. He said the museum library is open on Saturdays and there's a whole Cold War historiography shelf." He paused. "He also said the gallery closes in an hour, so maybe panic now."

The library turned out to be two rooms behind the member services desk, quiet enough that Maelle apologized to a chair for scraping it. The docent, whose lanyard read MR. PERERA, no relation she assumed, watched her run a finger along the spines. When she pulled down Gaddis and said she needed someone who disagreed with him, he nodded and slid a thick blue volume toward her.

"Try this one," he said quietly, because a woman at the next table was already glaring. "It won the Bancroft Prize in 1993. Fair warning, it's heavy in every sense."

The book was A Preponderance of Power, by Melvyn Leffler. She read the first chapter standing up, one hip against the shelf, while Callie sat on the floor under the window and Rohan took flashless photos of the footnotes for her. Leffler's argument, she saw slowly, was not that American leaders were villains or dupes. He argued that they pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world. Security through control. Gaddis, as she understood him from three nights of highlighting, saw containment as a defensive response, a fence built against expansion. Leffler saw the fence become an empire, or at least a system so wide that it was hard to call it a fence anymore.

"The Marshall Plan," Rohan said, reading over her shoulder. "Gaddis loves the Marshall Plan."

"Leffler loves it too, but not the way you mean." She showed him a page where the aid was described alongside American access to markets and resources, the whole arrangement less charity than architecture. "Okay, so here's my problem. If I write that Leffler says the US was profligate with money to buy influence, is that his point or is that me being cynical?"

"That's you," Callie said from the floor. "But you're allowed to be you as long as you label it."

Maelle laughed, surprising herself, and a laugh in a library made her lower her voice. She sat down at the empty table and opened her notebook, the one whose margins had metastasized into a second essay over the past week, arrows and question marks spreading until they crowded out the actual sentences. She wrote: Leffler, 1993 Bancroft, dominance as the road to security. Then she wrote underneath: But does the evidence decide it, or just the emphasis?

The problem was that the documents agreed with both of them. The Truman Doctrine spoke of free peoples; the same year's planning memos spoke of access and preponderance. She read for another hour while Callie fetched water for all three of them from the fountain down the hall, unprompted, and set the paper cup beside Maelle's elbow like an offering. Rohan photographed the arms-control timeline on the wall for his own class, and when he came back he said, "You know what's weird? Both guys think war didn't happen. They just argue about why."

That was the hinge, she thought, or wrote, underlining twice. Gaddis said the restraint worked. Leffler said the dominance worked, that preponderance bought caution, that rebuilding Germany and Japan was an indemnity paid forward so no one would want war again. She stopped. She was now doing the thing Mr. Perera had warned about, building a neat seesaw with two names on it, and the evidence didn't sit neatly on either end. Some memos, some speeches. Fear in some, appetite in others, fear and appetite in the same paragraph.

She wrote her conclusion in the notebook's last clean margin: Leffler's explanation fits the planning documents better; Gaddis's fits the public language; what stays uncertain is which language was the real one, or whether they were both real at once, and a seventeen-year-old in a museum library cannot settle that, only say it honestly.

At closing time Mr. Perera the docent unlocked the doors for them. Outside, the evening had gone blue and cold, and Callie offered Maelle half the last granola bar, which she took.

"Monday," Rohan said. "Tell me it's done."

"It's done being honest," Maelle said. "That's not the same as done." She zipped the notebook into her bag, where the thick blue book already waited, checked out on her brand-new library card, its spine cool against her palm through the canvas.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: Adding lanes to a congested highway often fails to reduce traffic for long, because faster trips attract more driving until the new space fills; this effect is called induced demand.
story:
The map on the wall of Room 114 had pins in it, and Alexia had been staring at the cluster of red pins along Route 9 for most of fourth period. Ms. Petrov had taped a newspaper clipping beside the pins, an article about the council meeting on Thursday, and under the clipping she had written a single question in green marker: Who benefits? The room smelled like dry-erase marker and the radiator's burnt dust, and outside the window the November light was the flat gray of a photograph taken without flash.

"Route 9," Leana said, dropping into the seat beside her and unwrapping a granola bar despite the no-food rule. "My dad's firm is bidding on the widening project. Four lanes to eight. He says it's the biggest contract of his year."

"That's the road my dad takes to work," Alexia said. "He sits on it for forty minutes every evening. He's been furious about it since I was little."

Damian leaned across the aisle, reticent as usual until he decided something was worth saying. "My aunt lives two blocks off Route 9. She says the noise already rattles her teacups." He paused. "She went to a meeting once and came home hoarse."

Ms. Petrov passed out the assignment sheet: attend the council meeting Thursday, or watch the recording, and write not about what was decided but about what the speakers wanted and why. "Systems do not sit still while we fix them," she said, which was the kind of thing she said that Alexia usually wrote down and only understood a week later.

Alexia went to the meeting because her father went, and she sat beside him in the folding chairs of the high school gymnasium, where the council met because the municipal building had mold. The room was hot and full. A man in a reflective vest spoke first, holding a traffic count above his head like a trophy: forty minutes of delay at peak, and growing. "Widen the road," he said, "and the delay disappears. It's simple math." The crowd applauded. Her father applauded, his hands clapping close to her ear, and Alexia felt the pull of it, the simple rightness of more space for all these impatient cars.

Then a woman from the transit coalition took the microphone. She was younger than the man in the vest, and less confident, and she kept pushing her hair behind her ear. "I want to talk about what happened in the cities that already widened their congested highways," she said. "The trips get faster for a little while, and then the faster trips attract more driving until the new space fills up again. The engineers have a name for it. It's called induced demand." A man near the back booed, softly, like he was embarrassed by himself.

"Induced demand," Alexia whispered, writing it on the back of the program, and her father glanced at her sideways. When the public comment period opened, he stood up. She watched him hold the microphone and talk about missing her birthday dinner twice because of traffic, about the road being a broken promise made forty years ago, and she watched the council members nod along, and she thought about how nobody had answered the transit woman. They hadn't said she was wrong. They had just stopped listening.

At school the next Monday, Leana cornered her by the lockers. "Damian says you're writing your paper against the widening. My dad says you've been talking to the transit people." Her voice had an edge Alexia hadn't heard before. "Eighty million dollars, Alexia. Jobs. My dad's whole season."

"I'm not against anything yet," Alexia said, which was mostly true. That night she spread her notes on the kitchen table: the traffic counts, the woman's line about faster trips attracting more driving until the new space fills, Damian's aunt's teacups, the applause in the gymnasium. Her father came through for water and stood reading over her shoulder. "You're not still on that," he said, but he stayed, and his hand rested on the back of her chair.

The twist came at the next meeting, two weeks later, when the council voted. They voted to widen the road anyway, six votes to one, and the one dissenting vote was the councilwoman whose district held Damian's aunt. Afterward, in the parking lot, Alexia found the transit woman struggling with a folding table in the wind, and helped her carry it to a hatchback. "You knew they'd vote for it," Alexia said. The woman laughed, a short, tired sound. "I knew the math. I didn't know the people. Jobs are real. Your friend's father needs a season of work, and no model predicts that." She shut the hatch. "You can be right about the road and still not know what to do about it."

Alexia's paper took her three drafts. In the first she argued against the widening, and it read like an acolyte copying a sermon she had heard in a gymnasium. In the second she tried to codify her position into rules, cost against benefit, noise against jobs, and the rules kept contradicting each other. In the final draft she wrote that the road would fill again, that the traffic would return, and that this was knowable and known, and still the council had reasons that were also real, and she did not yet know how a city holds both truths at once. She suspected nobody did. She suspected that was the actual subject of geography.

When she got the paper back, Ms. Petrov had written one comment in green marker, under the last line: "Sit with it." Alexia read it twice, then folded the paper and put it in the front pocket of her backpack, the pocket she saved for things she was not finished with. Outside, Leana was waiting by the buses, and when she saw Alexia she lifted a hand, hesitated, then waved anyway. Alexia waved back and started across the parking lot, the asphalt still holding the day's heat through her sneakers.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: A pencil's core is a mix of graphite and clay; more clay makes a harder pencil with lighter marks, marked H, and less clay makes a softer, darker one, marked B.
story:
The problem announced itself as a gray bloom across the chin of the man in the portrait. Jordan had spent the morning in his grandfather's back room, working from a photograph he'd taken last summer, and every time his hand crossed the paper it dragged shadow with it, so that the drawing looked less like a portrait than like something viewed through a dirty window. He sat back on the stool, blowing graphite dust off the page, and wondered whether the fault was in him or in the tool, and how you would even begin to tell the difference.

The photograph was pinned to the corkboard above the desk, his grandfather squinting into the garden with a trowel in one hand. Jordan was drawing it as a graduation gift, though gift felt like the wrong word for something he needed to give more than anyone needed to receive. The house had been empty since March, and their family was selling it in July, which meant the drawing was also a way of keeping something, a graphite argument that the room should continue to exist somewhere.

His phone buzzed on the desk. Martina had sent him a photo of her own sketch, a study of hands, and beneath it: why does mine look like it survived a flood. He sent back a picture of his smudged chin, and she replied with laughing faces and a question he couldn't answer: what grade are you using? Grade, like the pencil was a student. He turned his pencil and found letters on the barrel he'd never thought about, an H and a number, and understood that he didn't know what they meant or whether they mattered.

The tin was in the bottom drawer, under seed catalogs. His grandfather had kept his drafting kit from the plant where he'd worked thirty years, and Jordan remembered, suddenly and completely, an afternoon from when he was nine: the two of them at this same desk, his grandfather sharpening a pencil with a paring knife, long pale curls falling into his palm, saying only, the tools know more than you think, so ask them first. Jordan had thought it was a joke about pencils. Now he opened the tin and found a dozen of them, some marked H, some marked B, and no explanation at all.

So he asked them. He ruled test squares across a scrap of the same paper, one pencil after another, then dragged his thumb horizontally through all of them. The H-marked squares barely smudged; the B-marked ones smeared dark and wide. He tried again, pressing harder, and the pattern held: H meant hard and light, B meant soft and dark. Somewhere between the letters, presumably, the whole range of gray existed, and he found he could almost interpolate the middle grades from the two ends he'd tested, could predict what an HB square would look like before he drew it. He tested one. He was close.

He redrew the chin with the H pencil and the smudging stopped, but the marks were so faint the face looked like it was dissolving into fog. This was the trade, then: clean and light, or dark and doomed to smear. Martina arrived at four, having biked over, and stood over the page with her hands clasped behind her back like a museum visitor. "Yours is better," she said, "but it's timid. You did the whole thing in H because you're scared of the mess."

"Look at the tin," Jordan said. "B is soft and dark, H is hard and light. Clay, apparently. More clay makes the H ones harder." He held up the two pencils side by side, then, on an impulse, turned the portrait toward her. "What if the face is H, everything that has to stay still, and the background is B, where a little mess is fine?"

They worked until the light went orange. Martina laid down the dark garden in bold soft strokes and let her wrist carry the smudge where it wanted, and Jordan drew the face with his hard pencil, going over the lines twice, three times, until the gray deepened without bleeding. He could not decide whether the result was his or hers or the pencils', and he found he liked not deciding. Next door, Mr. Buchanan's sprinkler came on with its ticking rhythm, and Martina said, "He'll want a copy of that, you know. The old sagacious one. He used to sit with your grandfather for hours."

Jordan texted a photo of the finished drawing to his mother, then carried the tin back to the drawer, closed it, and took it out again. He set it in his backpack, between a notebook and his charger, and left the paper weighted on the desk with the seed catalogs on top.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In the UK, students apply to university through UCAS and can choose up to five courses, listed in no order of preference.
story:
The mailbox at the end of Alexander's driveway had a dented lid that had to be lifted with two fingers, and for three weeks he had lifted it the same way, twice a day, and found nothing but a pizza menu and a letter about gutter cleaning. Today there was an envelope with a Glasgow postmark, and he stood in the cold in his socks because he had run out without shoes, holding it unopened while his breath fogged the plastic window.

He had applied through UCAS, which Sofia had explained to him back in September over coffee that went cold between them. "You can choose up to five courses," she had said, tapping his notebook with her pen. "And here's the strange part. They're listed in no order of preference. Universities can't see which one you want most." He had written that down and then, characteristically, agonized over it anyway, because a list with no order still had to be chosen, and choosing was the thing he was bad at.

The envelope was thin. He knew the folklore about thin envelopes, and he also knew he had promised himself he wouldn't believe in folklore, and he stood there doing both at once. Ray's text arrived before he had broken the seal: "well? did it come? i'm dying over here." Ray had applied to one course, one city, a decision made in about four minutes that Alexander had spent a whole evening trying to talk him out of, and failing, and secretly admiring.

He opened it inside, at the kitchen table, with his mother pretending to dry the same plate. It was an acknowledgment, not a decision. His application was under review. His mother made a small sound, relief and disappointment braided together, and went back to the plate.

That night he took out the notebook again. Five courses: Glasgow, two in London, one in Manchester, one in St Andrews. He had built the list the way he built everything, by ranking and re-ranking, and then Sofia's voice came back to him, saying no order of preference, and he understood, for the first time, that the ranking had been for him, not for them. The universities would each see only their own course, blind to whether they were his first choice or his safety. He had been performing an order for an audience that didn't exist.

"It's like the form refuses to let you commodify it," he told Ray the next afternoon, at the wall behind the sports hall where they went to think out loud. Ray looked at him. "You can't shop around visibly. You can't signal. Five choices, no hierarchy, and nobody on the other end knows where they stand."

"Sounds efficient," Ray said.

"It sounds cruel, actually. Or honest. I can't decide which."

What he couldn't decide, more precisely, was whether the anonymity freed him or stranded him. If no university knew it was his first choice, then his first choice didn't matter as a signal, only as a fact, a thing true in him and nowhere else. He had spent years learning to arrange himself for inspection, applications and personal statements and a carefully edited self, and the form had quietly removed the market for it. There was a subtlety to the arrangement he was still turning over: the list said nothing about desire, and yet desire was the only thing that could determine what he did with the list, once the offers came or didn't.

Mr. Li, who had lived next door since Alexander was seven and who had emigrated from a country whose education system he described only as "less forgiving," was shovelling the last snow off his walk. Alexander, coming back from the mailbox empty-handed again, stopped at the fence.

"Did you hear?" Mr. Li said. "Glasgow took Ray's cousin in a day last year."

"Ray's cousin had three A-stars predicted."

"Ah." Mr. Li leaned on the shovel. "Then you are waiting on subtler arithmetic."

Alexander laughed, and then, because it was Mr. Li, said more than he meant to. "The worst part is I don't even know if I want Glasgow most. I think I chose St Andrews for the prestige and Glasgow for the city and I disguised each one as the other. If I get both I'll have to find out what I actually want with no form to blame."

"Forms are good for that," Mr. Li said. "Blaming." He went back to the snow.

The decision, when it came, came in stages over two weeks, each envelope a small negotiation between his mother's hopes and his own uncertainty, until he sat at the table with two offers in front of him and a reply deadline circled on the calendar in someone else's handwriting. He went to the mailbox one last time before deciding, as if it might weigh in, and found the pizza company had sent a second menu, glossy and moribund under the flap, advertising the same deal as before.

Sofia called while he was standing there. "Have you picked?"

"I've narrowed it to a method," he said. "I'm going to decide what I'd choose if no one ever found out where I ranked either one."

"That's not a method, that's a personality."

"Fine. Then it's my personality."

He put the menu in the recycling, and the empty mailbox stayed open behind him, lid lifted, filling slowly with the grey light off the snow. He looked at it for a moment, then closed it, and went inside to find a pen.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: Plain-language guidance recommends the active voice, in which the subject does the action, as in 'I missed the deadline', because it makes clear who did what.
story:
The invoice said forty bags of concrete mix, and Connor had keyed in fourteen, and a man named Mr. Harlow had driven forty minutes home before he noticed. Now Mr. Harlow's email sat open on the register computer, three paragraphs long, and Connor had read the phrase "unacceptable incompetence" four times before Ms. Siddiqui came over and stood beside him with her arms folded.

"You're going to reply," she said. "Not me. You."

"Shouldn't the company reply?"

"The company doesn't have hands," said Ms. Siddiqui. "You have hands. You typed the number. Draft it, show me, don't send anything until I've seen it."

She went back to the office, which everyone called the office although it was a desk behind a plastic tarp, and Connor sat on an upturned paint bucket and began composing in his head. His first instinct was elegance. Something like: Regrettably, an error was made in the processing of your order, and inconvenience was experienced. It had the smooth, blameless glide of the apology emails he got from the bus company whenever a route vanished. Nobody was in the sentence. Nobody could be sued, or excoriated in a reply, or made to feel bad at nine at night. He liked it enormously.
