Giuseppe arrived for his shift at four and read over Connor's shoulder, because personal boundaries were not among Giuseppe's many talents. "That's corporate," Giuseppe said, approving. "That's how banks talk. Nobody confesses in a bank letter."

"It's called the passive voice," said Gianluca, who was restacking the concrete bags, all forty of the correct ones that had arrived that morning. He was taciturn by nature, so when he kept talking they both shut up and listened. "The subject doesn't do anything. Plain-language guidance recommends the active voice instead. Subject does the action. Like 'I missed the deadline.' Makes clear who did what."

"You read plain-language guidance," said Giuseppe, "for fun."

"It's for my cousin's website. Also, it's obvious." Gianluca went back to the bags, conversation apparently complete.

Connor typed a second draft in the notes app on his phone. I entered your order incorrectly. I am sorry. The forty bags are here and I have set aside exactly forty, plus the two you originally asked about as an apology, if you want them, free. It was shorter. It was also terrifying. Every time he looked at the word "I" it seemed to lean out of the screen the way a person leans off a curb into traffic.

"It reads like a ransom note," Giuseppe said. "Like you're going to cut off a finger next."

"It reads like a person," said Gianluca from the aisle.

"You know what Mr. Harlow's going to do with a person? A person he can yell at. Corporate, nobody can yell at. Nobody is basically the customer-service firewall." Giuseppe was grinning, but Connor could hear the actual argument underneath it, because Giuseppe's father ran a body shop and had opinions about admitting fault, opinions delivered mainly through stories that ended with the word "lawyers."

Connor thought about the bus company again, about all the times a delay had been "experienced" and he had stood in the rain feeling that the rain itself was somehow more accountable than the company. He had never once felt apologized to. That was one way of thinking about it. The other way was Giuseppe's: the letter was not really for Mr. Harlow's feelings, it was for the file, for whoever might read it later with a lawyer attached. Two different purposes, and a sentence could only really serve one.

He took the phone to the tarp. Ms. Siddiqui read both drafts, the smooth one and the bare one, and her face did something small at the first one, not quite a wince, more the expression of a person who has bitten into a store-brand orange.

"The second," she said. "With one change. Take out 'free' on the extra bags and write 'no charge.' 'Free' sounds like a promotion. 'No charge' sounds like an apology." She handed the phone back. "You typed the number, you write the letter. Send it."

"I thought you had to approve."

"I just did. Go."

Connor sat on the paint bucket again and pressed send before the sentence could get any more dangerous. Then he went and helped Gianluca stack, because standing still felt impossible. The bags were heavy and dusty and the work had the good dumb rhythm of work that doesn't care about your email.

Mr. Harlow's reply came in at 6:40, while Connor was sweeping near the registers. Giuseppe read it aloud in a courtroom voice. "Thank you for the straightforward response. I will collect the order Saturday morning. Your employee who wrote this is the only person at any hardware store who has ever admitted a mistake to me in forty years." There was no exclamation point. There was no anger either. It sat there in the inbox, plain as a receipt.

"So we don't know if that's praise or a complaint," Giuseppe said.

"We don't," Connor said. He read it once more himself, then closed the register, counted the drawer, and wrote the total on the slip in the active voice, as it were, his own hand, his own numbers, initialed at the bottom. Saturday morning he would be the one at the loading door when Mr. Harlow pulled in, and he did not know yet what he would say, only that he would be the one saying it.

"Two extra bags," Gianluca said from the doorway, and put them on the dolly.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 2018 economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed the 1985 hot-hand analysis had a statistical bias and found evidence of streak shooting in the same data.
story:
The community center gym smelled of floor wax and old popcorn, and by the third week of the season Andrew had learned to arrive early enough to claim the good ball, the one whose grip hadn't gone slick. He was the sixth man on a team of eight, which meant he played when someone was tired or in foul trouble, and mostly he sat on the folding chair beside Kylee, who kept the book, writing down shots and misses in her tight, exact print.

Brock played point guard and thought about basketball the way other people thought about weather systems. He'd stay after practice shooting from the same spot until he'd made ten in a row, and he kept a spreadsheet on his phone that no one else was allowed to see. On the Thursday before the game against St. Gerard's, Mr. Khoury stopped practice and told the team to keep feeding the ball to whoever was hot, because you ride the hot hand, that's just how it works.

Brock, who was seventeen and had never once been circumspect about being right, said the hot hand wasn't real, that it had been studied and disproved. Mr. Khoury laughed and said he'd been coaching for twenty-two years. Brock got that flat look he got when he thought someone was being unscientific, and practice moved on, but the argument sat in the back of Andrew's mind and began to ferment there, the way questions do when nobody bothers to answer them properly.

That night he texted Kylee, who found things the way she found typos in the book, without seeming to look. She sent back a message with a screenshot and a line of her own: "In 2018 economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed the 1985 hot-hand analysis had a statistical bias and found evidence of streak shooting in the same data." Andrew read it three times. He didn't understand all of it, but he understood enough to know that Brock's certainty was out of date, that the old study that had called the hot hand a myth had a flaw in it, and that the same data, looked at correctly, showed the streaks were real. Both of them had been holding half of something.

The St. Gerard's game was close for three quarters and then stopped being close in the wrong direction. Andrew went in with four minutes left when the starter in front of him rolled an ankle, and his first shot, a corner three he took without thinking, went down clean. His second went in too, and something opened up in his chest, a loosening, the hoop looking suddenly like a bucket. On the bench he could hear Mr. Khoury yelling to give it to Andrew, and behind that, Brock calling for the ball to come back to him, because Brock believed the run meant nothing, that the next shot had no memory of the last one.

Andrew took the third shot because it was the honest shot, the defense sagging off him, and he made it. Then he missed two in a row, and the feeling closed again like water over a stone. St. Gerard's pulled away and won by nine, and in the handshake line the boy guarding him said nice stroke, kid, and Andrew didn't know whether to believe him.

Afterward, in the lobby where the vending machines hummed, Brock was waiting by the water fountain with his phone out, ready to relitigate everything. Andrew got there first. He said that he'd looked it up, that Miller and Sanjurjo had found the bias in the old analysis in 2018, that the streaks showed up in the same data. Brock stared at him and said that wasn't fair, Andrew wasn't supposed to have ammunition. Kylee, folding the scorebook into her backpack, said she was the ammunition, and that they could both thank her later.

They sat on the folding chairs while the janitor pushed the mop in long, patient arcs across the court. Brock argued that even if the streaks were real, you couldn't know in the moment whether you were in one, and Andrew found he agreed with that part, that knowing the thing existed was different from knowing where you stood inside it. He had made three in a row and then missed two, and he could not have said which of those shots the truth had been about. Mr. Khoury came through on his way out and told them to lock up when they left, and paused long enough to say that Andrew's fourth quarter had won them the game if the other three quarters hadn't lost it.

Brock bounced a ball twice against the floor and caught it, looking at the far hoop as if it were a problem he intended to solve by morning. "Same data," he said. "Next season I'm charting everything. You, me, all of it." He tossed Andrew the ball. "Shoot from the corner. Where you were hot." Andrew stood, spun the ball once in his hands, and set his feet at the line.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: When the US House and Senate pass different versions of a bill, a conference committee of members from both chambers can write a compromise, which both chambers must then pass.
story:
Sydney opened the laptop at the kitchen table at nine forty at night, while her mother washed dishes behind her, and logged into the joint council call. Her draft had started three weeks ago as a single sentence on the same screen: Students at both campuses should be allowed to eat lunch in the library on exam days. It had gone to her campus council's rules committee first, where Angelica had moved to strike "on exam days," and Lea had moved to add "quiet study zone," and by the end of an hour the sentence had three clauses and a semicolon it had not been born with. Then everyone had voted on it, and it had passed, and Sydney had felt that particular pride of watching something you typed become something other people argued over.

Behind the dishes, her mother asked whether she was doing homework. "Sort of," Sydney said, and it wasn't even a lie, exactly.

The complication was the other campus. Their council had taken the same idea, because Lea had a cousin over there and ideas traveled, and they had passed their own version, which Sydney had read at eleven the night before with her heart beginning to palpitate in a way she distrusted: no semicolon, no quiet study zone, and lunch banned outright in favor of morning passes before first period. Two versions of one rule. On the shared chat, someone had written, in a tone that could only be described as vitriolic for people arguing about a library, that the other campus "clearly doesn't read."

"Can you hear me?" asked Ms. Kang, the advisor who had agreed to sit in on the joint session only if the students ran it themselves. Her camera showed a bookshelf and half a cat.

"Yes," said everyone, at slightly different times, so it came out "ye y es yes."

Sydney had prepared for this. That afternoon, unable to stop herself, she had done what she always did when a problem had no obvious shape: she looked up how it was done at scale. She'd found, in a government textbook site that still smelled, metaphorically, of someone else's highlighter, the thing she now had open in a second tab. When the House and the Senate pass different versions of a bill, a conference committee made up of members from both chambers can write a compromise, which both chambers then have to pass. She read it twice, then once more, because it seemed almost too convenient, like finding out that the adult world had already invented a container for exactly your problem.

She thought of her father, who traced their family's genealogy on weekends and liked to say that every family argument had been held before, by other people, with worse record-keeping. Rules, she was beginning to suspect, worked the same way.

"Here's the thing," she said, unmuting. "They do this in Congress. When the House and Senate pass different versions of a bill, a conference committee, members from both chambers, writes a compromise. Then both chambers have to pass it."

"Why would we copy Congress," said a boy from the other campus, whose name she'd forgotten twice already, "Congress can't pass anything."

A pause in which Sydney did not say several things. "Because it gives us one version instead of two," she said finally, "and nobody's version gets to just win."

They picked three from each campus, Sydney and Lea and Angelica on one side, and the debate began. Lea fought for the quiet study zone with the persistence of rain. Angelica, surprisingly, conceded the semicolon, saying she'd only added it to see whether anyone would notice. The morning-passes delegate from the other campus turned out to be less hostile than his chat messages, and mostly worried that tuna sandwiches would be near the rare books, which, Sydney admitted, was a real category of worry.

The room went quiet then, and Sydney let it, because the compromise was sitting in her document cursor, half-written, and she could see both ways it could go. Keep "exam days," and the rule was small and would pass easily and mean almost nothing. Drop it, and the library changed for everyone, and the librarian, who was not on the call and had not been asked, would come in some morning to find her desk smelling like a cafeteria.

Lea's hand, metaphorically, hovered over the chat. "So do we cut exam days?"

Sydney typed the sentence, deleted it, typed it again. "We cut it," she said, "but we add cleanup duty, rotating, by grade." She was not certain this was the right call. She was certain it was hers, which she had begun to suspect was the more useful kind of certainty.

They voted on the compromise in the committee, five to one, the tuna delegate abstaining dramatically. Then each campus caucused separately to pass or reject it, and Sydney sat with her camera off, listening to the muffled counting from the other room's breakout call, her hand flat on the table beside the keyboard.

The other campus came back first. "Passed," their chair said. "Eighteen to four. The four want it noted that they were right about the tuna."

Sydney unmuted her own campus and called the vote, and watched the hands, digital and literal, go up on the screen.

"All right," she said, when the count was done, and screen-shared the final version. "One rule, one text. Ms. Kang, does the principal just sign this, or do we print it?"

"Print two," Ms. Kang said. "She likes a copy for the wall."

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: In his 1961 book Griff nach der Weltmacht, German historian Fritz Fischer argued that Imperial Germany deliberately pursued a world war, setting off a long debate known as the Fischer controversy.
story:
Emile had both textbooks open on the desk beside the keyboard, their spines cracked at the same week in July 1914. His own book, the one from school, said the war's origins lay in a tangle of alliances and mobilization schedules, no single nation fully responsible. Giselle's book, which she had lent him after class because she was going to Paris for the weekend and would not need it, said something sharper: that Germany had sought the war, that the evidence pointed to intention rather than accident. He sat transfixed by the two paragraphs, reading one, then the other, then the first again, as though the screen between them might arbitrate.

He typed the difference into the search bar, more out of frustration than method. The results came up in German first, then English: a name, Fritz Fischer, and a book with a title he could not pronounce. In his 1961 book Griff nach der Weltmacht, Fischer had argued that Imperial Germany deliberately pursued a world war. Emile read the sentence twice. He had expected the internet to tell him which book was right. Instead it told him the argument itself was the event.

He opened a message window and typed to Giselle, who was, according to her status, online despite the packing she claimed to be doing. "Your textbook isn't wrong," he wrote. "It's just taking a side." Then he deleted that, because it sounded like an accusation, and wrote instead: "Did you know there's a whole thing about this? It has a name and everything."

In her bedroom across town, Giselle sat on the floor with a half-closed suitcase and the phone against her knee. She read Emile's message, then the follow-up: "It's called the Fischer controversy." She knew the tone underneath his careful typing, the way he circled a question for hours before landing on it, and she suspected this one had been circling since their teacher, Mr. Moose, had split the class over the essay prompt. She also suspected that Emile had found the German book before she had, and that this pleased him more than he would admit.

"Fischer," she typed back. "Is he the one with the beard?" "Everyone in 1961 had a beard," Emile wrote. "The point is it never ended. People are still arguing." There was a pause, the typing indicator appearing and vanishing twice, which Giselle recognized as Emile drafting and discarding something more honest. When the message came, it was plain: "My book barely mentions him. Yours makes him the whole answer. How are we supposed to write the same essay?"

She set the phone down and looked at the suitcase. Her mother had offered, more than once, to make this trip a kind of graduation gift, and Giselle had accepted without examining what was being exchanged for it: a summer of appointments her mother arranged like a sinecure, effortless and slightly deadening, in exchange for the ticket. She did not say any of this. She picked the phone back up and wrote, "Maybe that's the essay. Not who caused it. Why the answer keeps moving."

Emile leaned back. His father passed the doorway with laundry and paused long enough to read the two open textbooks upside down, which he could not, and to say, "Still on the war? You've been on the war since Tuesday." Emile said it was due Monday, and his father said Monday came fast, and went on down the hall with the basket.

Matthieu called at nine, belligerent about a referee decision in the match he had just watched, and spent four minutes on the penalty before asking what Emile was doing. When Emile explained the two textbooks, Matthieu said, "So one of them is lying." Emile said no, that was the thing; both were using the same archives, roughly, and both were honest, and the disagreement had been running since Fischer published. "Then it's unanswerable," Matthieu said, and Emile found himself objecting, surprising himself with the force of it. Not unanswerable. Partially answered. The sources that survived were partial, the questions people asked changed with the times, and a book written in 1961 Germany was answering its own country as much as answering 1914.

He wrote none of that in the message to Giselle, only: "I think I know my thesis. Or the shape of one. I'm still not sure which book I trust more, if either." Then he pulled the keyboard closer and opened a blank document. The cursor blinked in the empty field for a while. He typed the first line, deleted the word "obviously" from it, and left the rest standing.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as those observed if there were truly no effect; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
story:
Keira spread the two articles across the corner table by the library's tall windows, weighting the first with her keys so it would stay open. One claimed that later school start times improved adolescent attendance; the other, using a different district and a different method, found no effect worth mentioning. Her assignment, due Thursday, was to compare them and take a position, and she had been circling the paragraph that bothered her for most of an hour. In the margin of her notebook she had copied the sentence: the significant result meant the start-time study was 95 percent likely to be right. She had written it herself, two nights ago, and now it sat there looking less like a sentence and more like a door she had painted shut.

Shayne dropped into the chair across from her with a stack of magazines and a granola bar that crumbled the moment it touched the table. "Still on that paper?" he said, brushing the crumbs into his palm. "You've had those same two pages out since Tuesday."

"I wrote something I can't defend," Keira said. She turned the notebook so he could see. "The article says the result was significant at p equals 0.05, and I said that means there's a 95 percent chance the hypothesis is true. But I can't actually find anything in either paper that says that, and when I say it out loud it sounds like I'm guessing."

Shayne read the margin, chewing. "Isn't that what the number means? Five percent chance they're wrong, ninety-five percent chance they're right. That's how I'd write it."

"That's how everyone would write it," Keira said. "That's the problem."

She pulled the statistics chapter of her brother's old textbook toward her, the one she had carried in as an afterthought and had not opened until now. The chapter on hypothesis testing was dense, and the first three definitions were tangential to what she needed, full of vocabulary about samples and populations that circled the actual question without landing on it. She skipped ahead. Somewhere in the middle of the page, one sentence stopped her, and she read it three times, once silently, once under her breath, once out loud to Shayne without quite meaning to.

"The p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as the ones they got," she said slowly, "if there were truly no effect. It's not the probability that the hypothesis is true. It's not even about the hypothesis being true. It's about the data. Assuming nothing is going on, how weird would these numbers be." She sat back. "So my sentence isn't just clumsy. It's backwards."

"So the 0.05 means what, then?" Shayne said.

"If start times actually did nothing, there'd be a five percent chance of seeing a difference that big or bigger anyway." She tapped the article. "The study didn't prove anything true. It measured how surprised we should be."

At the reference desk, Ms. Zhang was checking in a cart of returns, and Keira waited through two patrons before asking whether the library had anything on interpreting statistics for non-statisticians. Ms. Zhang led her past the externality of the quiet study room, where a book club had overrun its hour and the murmur of argument leaked into the stacks, and pulled down a slim guide to reading research. "The chapter on inference gets checked out by nursing students mostly," Ms. Zhang said, handing it over. "It's good on what numbers can and cannot abrogate, if that makes sense. People want a study to settle an argument for them. It rarely does."

Keira carried the guide back to the window. The second article, the null one, had used a larger sample, which she now understood cut both ways: a bigger study could detect a smaller effect, but it could also drown a real one in noise if the effect depended on the district, the students, the year. The two papers weren't simply disagreeing about a fact. They were asking different versions of the question, in different places, with different amounts of power to notice anything at all. She wrote that down, then crossed out her margin sentence and replaced it with a plainer one: the first study showed results that would be unlikely if start times had no effect at all.

She did not know which district generalize to hers, or whether attendance was even the outcome that mattered, and she wrote that too, at the bottom of the page, as a kind of debt to be honest about. Shayne had drifted to the magazines, and the light through the tall windows had moved from the tabletop to the floor. Keira squared the two articles, put the textbook in her bag, and left the library guide open to the inference chapter, her pen resting in the crease.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Gar Alperovitz argued in Atomic Diplomacy (1965) that the atomic bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union.
story:
The bus parked in gravel lot below the memorial, and Mya got off holding two photocopies she had not yet read, one in each back pocket like playing cards she was hiding. Mr. Müller had assigned them the night before: a chapter from a textbook that called the atomic bombings of 1945 the decisive end of World War II, and an excerpt from Gar Alperovitz, who argued in Atomic Diplomacy, published in 1965, that the bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union. Her task, written on the board in his narrow handwriting, was to weigh the two explanations against the evidence and say which one the evidence favored. She had a draft due Monday. She had, so far, a title and one sentence she already suspected was wrong.

The memorial sat on a bluff above the harbor, a granite wall with names carved into it in rows so regular they looked machine-cut. Layton reached the wall first and ran his thumb along one of the engraved letters, the way people did when they wanted to seem solemn without having to feel anything in particular. David stood a few feet back with his hands in his pockets, which was his way of announcing that he had a position and was waiting to be asked for it.

"Okay," Layton said, turning around. "Since we're stuck here for two hours. Last act of the Second War or first act of the Cold War. Pick a side."

"That's a false framing," David said.

"It's a Tuesday framing. Pick."

Mya took out the photocopies. The wind snapped at them, and she had to pin the corners with her fingers. "I can't pick yet. That's the whole assignment. Alperovitz says the bombs were used partly to intimidate the Soviet Union. Partly. That's a smaller claim than you two are making on either side."

Layton waved this off. "Alperovitz is grandiose. Every revisionist wants to be the guy who proved the war was really about the next one. It sells books."

"He's not being grandiose if the documents support him," Mya said. "Grandiose would be claiming more than the documents support. I haven't seen the documents yet. Neither have you."

"You're pathologizing him," David said mildly. "You're treating an argument you dislike as a symptom of his personality instead of answering it."

Layton rolled his eyes, but Mya wrote pathologizing in the margin of the excerpt, because it was useful to name the move she knew she was about to make herself. She recognized the temptation. The textbook explanation was clean and finished, a door closing on a war; Alperovitz's was a door opening onto fifty years of standoff, and it made the story sadder in a way that felt almost voyeuristic, as though you wanted the tragedy to be bigger than it was. She caught herself preferring the smaller tragedy for aesthetic reasons and wrote that down too, in smaller letters, where no one would see it.

They walked the length of the wall while Mr. Müller trailed behind the group, answering a question from someone's mother about the dates on the base. Mya read as she walked. The textbook chapter gave casualty projections for an invasion and the demands already issued to Japan; it made the decision look like arithmetic, terrible arithmetic, done by exhausted men. The Alperovitz excerpt was denser, heavier with footnotes, and careful in a way she had not expected. It did not claim the Soviet Union was the only reason. It did not even claim it was the main reason, not in the pages she had. Partly, the word kept recurring, partly, like a man placing stones carefully rather than throwing them.

"Here's my problem," she said aloud, when the three of them had drifted to the far end of the wall, away from the others. "Both of them can be true. The bombs ended the war and they intimidated the Soviets. Men can do one thing for more than one reason. My dad took the job in Cleveland for the money and to be closer to his mother, and he'd tell you both, and he wouldn't be lying either time."

"Then your essay says both and you get a B," Layton said. "Müller wants a considered position."

"A considered position can hold two things," David said.

"Then it's subterfuge," Layton said. "It's hiding behind complexity. Pick the stronger one. Subterfuge is still subterfuge if you call it nuance."

Mya looked at the wall while they argued, and the names stopped looking machine-cut. The rows were regular but the letters varied, deeper in places, as though different hands had done the cutting across different years, and she thought that was closer to the truth than either of her two essays-in-waiting. The evidence would not line up in rows. Some of it would cut deep, some would barely scratch the surface, and the honest thing was to say which and where.

Mr. Müller came over, glanced at the photocopies fanned out in her hands, and did not offer an opinion, which she understood was itself a kind of instruction. "Monday," was all he said. "Weigh it. You're allowed to leave the scale trembling."

On the bus home, Layton slept against the window and David listened to something through one earbud, offering her the other. She took it, and while the music ran she turned the Alperovitz excerpt over and wrote across the back of the last page: the intimidation of the Soviet Union was real and partly causal; the ending of the war was real and possibly sufficient; the scale trembles. Then she crossed out possibly, wrote probably, crossed that out too, and left the space blank. Outside, the harbor dropped behind a hill, and she folded the papers along a fresh crease and put them in the front pocket, where she could reach them.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird, a black cat peers over Kahlo's shoulder, usually interpreted as a symbol of bad luck and death.
story:
The waiver on the clipboard said that signing it would indemnify the studio against any injury suffered on the premises, and Jeremy signed it without reading past the first clause, the way he had signed his sister's permission forms all year, the way he signed everything. Ms. Clarke took the clipboard back and pointed him toward the long table where Miya and Korbin were already leaning over a stack of prints.

"Thorn Necklace," she said. "Frida Kahlo. You've got an hour to write a formal analysis before we discuss. Colour, composition, symbolism. No googling until after."

Jeremy sat down between them and pulled a print toward him. Last semester he had written an essay about a poem for Ms. Clarke's class and gotten the only A she gave, and he had felt for months that the grade had indemnified him, somehow, against ever being wrong in her room again. Now he stared at the painting and understood how little that A was worth here. A woman in the jungle, a necklace of thorns sunk into her neck, a hummingbird hanging black and still from it, butterflies in her hair, a monkey tugging at the thorns.

Korbin had his pen out and was doing what Korbin always did, listing. "Monkey on the right shoulder, playing with the thorns. Black cat, behind her, over her shoulder, just its head and eyes. Dragonflies up top. The bird."

"Stop," Miya said. "That's inventory, not analysis."

"It's the middle step," Korbin said. "You inventory, then you interpret."

"Then interpret. What is the cat doing there?"

The question sat on the table between them. Jeremy looked at the cat again, its eyes pale and wide above Kahlo's shoulder, and something in the way it watched the viewer rather than the painter unsettled him. He thought of the photograph above his grandmother's stove, a savanna stretched gold under a thin sky, the picture she had brought with her when she emigrated and had never once explained. When he was eight he had asked what the animals in it were doing there and she had said, "Watching," and gone back to her pot, and he had spent years deciding that meant nothing and then a year deciding it meant everything.

"There's a reading where it's simple," Jeremy said slowly. "Black cat over the shoulder. Bad luck and death. That's what people usually take it as. It's not even hidden, it's right behind her, looking out at us like it's on her side of the painting but working for ours." He heard himself and stopped, unsure whether he had said something or borrowed it.

"Usually interpreted," Miya said, reading off her phone under the table. "Yeah. That's the standard note."

"You googled before the hour," Korbin said.

"I googled the second he said it, because he said it like he was sure." She put the phone face down. "That's the difference. I'm not sure. I think the monkey picking at the thorns complicates it. If the cat means death, the monkey means something trying to undo the hurt, and they're both animals she invited in. So which one is she?"

Jeremy wrote none of this down. Instead he found himself arguing the other side of himself, the way he had all spring with his father about the move, one night saying a fresh start was cowardice and the next saying staying was just being obdurate. "Or she doesn't choose," he said. "The background is green, the whole thing, green leaves behind her like a wall. Green behind, black over the shoulder, blood at the throat. Composition puts the death and the growth in the same frame and gives neither one more room."

"That's composition," Korbin admitted, "and colour."

"And symbolism," Miya said, "if you don't pretend it resolves."

Ms. Clarke came around the table and looked at their pages. Korbin had a full inventory. Miya had three paragraphs. Jeremy had four sentences and then a blank half page, and he covered it with his forearm before he could stop himself, a reflex from years of wanting the finished thing to appear fully formed.

"Blank space is fine," she said. "What's in the four sentences?"

"That the cat is the usual symbol, bad luck and death, but the painting puts it beside a monkey that undoes harm, and I don't know yet which one she'd claim, and I don't think the painting knows either."

Ms. Clarke was quiet long enough that he looked up. She had her hand on the back of Miya's chair and she was looking at the cat's pale eyes, not at him.

"Write that," she said. "The part where you don't know. Don't fix it before dinner."

He lifted his forearm off the page and wrote one more line, then put the pen down and turned the print so the cat was facing Miya.

"Okay," he said. "You be the monkey. Argue the thorns can come out."

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: A 2019 study led by Ziad Obermeyer found a widely used US health-care algorithm underestimated Black patients' needs because it used past medical spending as a stand-in for how sick patients were.
story:
Maya's grandmother set the envelope beside her plate before she touched the food, the way other people said grace. It was from her health plan, thick paper, the kind that arrived when something had been decided about you. Maya's father ladled rice onto his own plate and then onto his mother's without being asked, because Grandma's wrist ached on cold evenings and she would sooner skip the rice than admit it.

"Are you going to open it or just guard it?" Maya's father said. Grandma pushed it an inch toward the center of the table, then back. "It's about that care program," she said. "The nurse who calls. They said I might qualify for extra help at home." Her voice was casual, but she had put on her good cardigan for dinner, and she only did that when she wanted to look like someone things went well for.

Maya had been half-listening, her phone face-down on her knee, but the word "qualify" reached her. Two weeks ago her computer science class had gone on a field trip to a company that built the software hospitals used to manage patients, and a girl named Talia had raised her hand during the Q and A. Talia was the kind of person who asked what everyone else was too polite to. "How does an engineer know what a data label really measures?" she had asked. "You can label something 'need,' but is that what the numbers are actually saying?" The engineer had paused, and instead of the smooth answer Maya expected, he told them about a study led by a doctor named Ziad Obermeyer. In 2019, Obermeyer's team examined a widely used health-care algorithm across the United States, and it turned out the algorithm underestimated Black patients' needs. The reason, he said, was that it used past medical spending as a stand-in for how sick patients were.

"Read it to us," Maya's father said now, and Grandma made a sound of protest, then smoothed the page open on the tablecloth. Maya commandeered the second page before Grandma could stack it back into order, and read while her grandmother read the first aloud. The program was called CareBridge. The letter said her application had been placed in a lower-priority review tier. Attached was a sheet of financial categories, and there, in the small print, was the word indigent, a box checked beside it. Grandma's spending record had been pulled as part of the review.

Maya's stomach went strange. She thought of the envelopes in the drawer by Grandma's TV, the ones she'd found while hunting for batteries last summer. Grandma skipped appointments when the copays stacked up. She filled her prescriptions every other month instead of every month. She had raised three kids on a secretary's pay and treated doctors the way she treated taxis, a luxury you called only when you absolutely could not walk. All those careful years had become a number, and the number had become a label, and the label was now saying she needed less help, not more.

"Is something wrong with the rice?" her father asked, because Maya had stopped eating. She told them about the field trip, about Talia's question, about the engineer's answer, repeating it slowly so she wouldn't get it wrong: the study had found that the algorithm underestimated Black patients' needs because it used past medical spending as a stand-in for how sick patients were. Grandma spent little. Therefore the machine believed she was barely sick at all.

"That's not the same thing," her father said. "Your grandmother's case could be anything. You don't know they even use that algorithm." He said it gently, the way he said most hard things, and Maya knew he was partly right, which was the worst part. She didn't know. The letter named no algorithm; it named only a tier. But she also knew that "you don't know" was what people said to make an unfair thing feel like a mysterious thing, and those were not the same either. "Maybe not," she said. "But somebody at that clinic does know, and they're not going to ask themselves unless somebody asks them first." Her father was quiet, pushing food around. Grandma said, to Maya's surprise, "I'd like to know why they called me indigent before they called me sick."

After dinner, while her father washed dishes he would normally have left for morning, Maya typed a message to Talia on her phone. "You know that question you asked the engineer? My grandma got a letter tonight, lower priority for home care, and I think it's the spending thing. I don't have proof. But her records are all skipped appointments and half-filled prescriptions. Can I use the name of that study in a letter to her clinic? I want to say it right." Talia's reply came before Maya had finished clearing her plate: "Obermeyer, 2019. Cite it exactly. And send me a copy, I want to show Mr. Koné." Maya found a clean sheet of paper, because Grandma trusted paper more than screens, and wrote at the top, "To the Patient Review Office of CareBridge." Then she looked across the table, and Grandma had put her glasses on and pulled the letter toward herself again, following the lines with one finger, like a woman checking a bill for an error.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Hydroplaning happens when a layer of water builds up between the tires and the road so the car loses traction; easing off the accelerator can let the tires regain grip.
story:
The rain had started before Alexa fastened her seatbelt, a thin steady drizzle that beaded on Ms. Ong's windshield and made the quiet street look like it had been drawn in pencil and then smudged. Ms. Ong lived three doors down and had offered, back in June, to teach her in the old Honda before Alexa's road test on Thursday, and today was Tuesday, which left them two evenings and a decision.

"Hands at nine and three," Ms. Ong said. "Not ten and two, they changed it. Everything about driving, they change it eventually."

Alexa turned the key. The engine caught, and the car shuddered under her like something waking up. She had read the manual twice, cover to cover, and she had watched her father drive for years with the patient attention of someone memorizing a language, and yet the steering wheel in her own hands felt entirely new, heavier than it looked.

"Forward to the end of the street, then a left," Ms. Ong said. She checked her watch, an ascetic little thing with a plain leather band and no adornments, the only jewelry she ever wore. "I promised the pharmacy I'd cover the evening shift at seven. So we have forty minutes, and we use them."

Kyra had texted four times on the walk over. Alexa had silenced the phone in her pocket, but she could feel it there like a debt. Kyra wanted her to drive them both to the mall on Thursday, immediately after the road test, because Kyra's mother worked until nine and there was a boy who worked the shoe store counter until eight-thirty and Kyra had a whole circumlocution prepared for why they needed to go, one reason folded inside another, none of them the actual reason. Alexa had said maybe. She was beginning to understand that "maybe" was its own kind of lie.

The wipers swept and swept. She made the left turn too widely, corrected, overcorrected, and Ms. Ong said nothing, which was somehow worse than being corrected. They came to the low stretch of Colvin Road where the pavement dipped and the storm drains always clogged, and the rain had gathered there in a long dark sheet, and Alexa, wanting to prove something to the silence, did not slow down.

The steering went light under her hands.

It was a sensation she had no word for and would never forget: the wheel suddenly turning without consequence, the car drifting left with a dreamy indifference, as though the road had been withdrawn and replaced with something smoother. Her arms wanted to wrench the wheel, every instinct in her body wanted to grab control and take it back, and somewhere underneath the panic a small remembered sentence surfaced, from page 112 of the manual she'd read at the kitchen table: hydroplaning, the layer of water between the tires and the road.

"Alexa," Ms. Ong said, quietly, not a command.

Alexa eased her foot off the accelerator. Not braking, not swerving, just letting the speed fall away on its own, holding the wheel where it was while the Honda drifted and drifted and then, with a shudder she felt in her teeth, the tires found the pavement again. The steering weighted her hands once more. The car tracked straight. She breathed out so hard the windshield fogged a little at the corner.

"How did you know to do that?" Ms. Ong asked.

"I read it. The water builds up under the tires so you lose traction, and if you ease off the gas, they can grip again." Alexa's voice came out steadier than she'd expected. "I didn't actually know I knew it until just now."

Ms. Ong nodded slowly, looking out at the wet street, the maples along it dark and dripping. "That's most of driving," she said. "Knowing it in your hands before you know it in your head."

They pulled to the curb outside the pharmacy at 6:52. The rain had softened to a mist that adumbrated, faintly, the shapes of the streetlamps coming on early down the block. Alexa sat with the engine ticking and thought about Thursday, and the road test, and Kyra's folded reasons. She took out her phone and looked at the last message, a photo of a dress with the caption "PLEASE," and she understood that she could pass the test and still not be the driver Kyra imagined, or wanted, and that the two things her hands had just held together, the knowledge and the nerve, were not the same as saying yes.

She typed, "I'll know Thursday," and put the phone face down on the seat.

"Turn it off," Ms. Ong said, gathering her coat. "Same time tomorrow. We'll do the hill start and the parallel park, and if it rains again, we'll find that puddle on purpose." She opened the door, then paused with one foot on the wet pavement. "You know what you did back there wasn't luck."

Alexa watched her cross the sidewalk and push through the pharmacy door, its bell ringing thin against the rain. Then she put the car in reverse, checking the mirror twice, and eased back onto the empty street alone.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Pomp and Circumstance became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905, where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music.
story:
The lobsters had been steaming since four, and by the time Emilie arrived from rehearsal, still smelling of the band room's chalky heat, the table at her grandmother's house was already a landscape of melted butter and arguing uncles. Her mother had taped a paper sign to the front door that read CONGRATULATIONS EMILIE, and beneath it, in smaller letters, because her mother could never leave anything alone, CLASS OF EVERYTHING. Emilie stood on the porch for a moment with her trombone case in one hand and the folded program in the other, deciding whether to be pleased.

The problem was the march. Tomorrow she would stand on the football field with the rest of the band and play "Pomp and Circumstance" for a graduating class of three hundred, and for three days she had been unable to stop wondering why. Why that song, at every school, in every movie about schools, in every cartoon where a dog receives a diploma. She had asked Mr. Ba after rehearsal, and he had only smiled and said, "Look it up, Miss Emilie. It's better when you find it yourself," which was his infuriating habit of turning every question into an assignment.

"You're hovering," said Kathleen, who had come to dinner because Kathleen came to every dinner, and had already claimed the chair nearest the potato salad. "Sit. Tell me why your face is doing that."

"I'm not doing a face."

"You're doing the face you do when Anis expatiates about his chess openings. That face. What is it?"

Emilie sat, ladled herself a portion of everything, and laid the folded program on the tablecloth beside her plate like evidence. "The march. Everyone plays it. Every graduation in the country, probably the world, plays the exact same piece of music, and nobody seems to know why. I asked Anis and he said, and I quote, 'tradition,' which is what people say when they don't know."

"It's probably just old," said her uncle from the head of the table, gesturing with a claw. "Everything at graduations is old. The robes, the Latin, all of it. They like to make you feel like you're joining something ancient. Meanwhile you're joining a student loan." He was, Emilie had decided at twelve, a demagogue of the dinner table: not malicious, exactly, but constitutionally incapable of letting a sentiment pass without mounting it like a podium.

Her phone was in her pocket. She took it out under the table, thumbing past the congratulatory texts, and typed the question into the search bar while Kathleen watched over her shoulder with the shamelessness of a seagull. The answer arrived in a paragraph of plain text, and Emilie read it twice, because the first time she had been sure she'd misread the date.

"It became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905," she said, looking up. "Where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music." She said it slowly, testing the shape of it. "That's it. That's the whole reason. One school played it once, for the composer, and then everybody just... copied Yale."

There was a pause in which the only sound was her grandmother cracking a claw with the serene violence of a woman who had done it for seventy years. Then Kathleen started laughing, and Emilie found she was laughing too, quietly, into her napkin.

"Do you understand what this means?" Emilie said. "I've been standing in the sun for three days thinking I was participating in something with roots, something metamorphic, like the robes, like the actual rocks. And it's a trend. It's a hundred-year-old trend that started because one university wanted to flatter a famous visitor. Half of what feels permanent is just somebody's idea that got stuck."

Her grandmother set down her claw. "Or," she said, "it's a piece of music so beautiful that once people heard it in that setting, they couldn't bear to let it go. Stuck isn't the only way to describe something that lasts."

Emilie considered this while the uncles resumed their debate about whether her cousin's new truck counted as a graduation gift or a loan. Both things could be true, she thought, and neither canceled the other: the tradition was an accident, and the accident had survived because it deserved to. She did not know which mattered more, and she suspected she wouldn't know for years, possibly not until she was the aunt at some other table making pronouncements over the lobster. That felt less like a failure than like the actual size of the thing.

After dinner she carried the folding chairs out to the porch, because in this family nobody was allowed to leave until the furniture was stacked. Kathleen followed with the leftover lemon cake and two forks. The sky over the harbor had gone the color of a bruise healing, and somewhere down the street a sprinkler ticked its slow circle.

"Play me a bit," Kathleen said, mouth full. "The march. On the porch. Right now."

So Emilie opened the case, wet her lip, and played the first eight bars into the dark street, slow and true, while the sprinkler kept time.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Hanukkah menorah has nine branches: eight for the nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others, one more each night.
story:
The park had been claimed by folding tables and a rented generator, and by the time Benjamin's family arrived, the menorah stood on the bandstand like a small brass tree waiting for leaves. It was the fourth night of Hanukkah, and the community center had moved the celebration outdoors this year, stringing lights between the oaks so that the whole lawn glowed the color of weak tea. His mother carried the sufganiyot in a tin that had once held sewing supplies. His father carried a folding chair and his opinions about folding chairs.

Benjamin had been given the job of candles. Four of them, plus the shamash, which was why he'd been repeating the arithmetic since the car: four plus the helper, five in his hand, walk up when Ms. López calls the families. Ms. López taught English at the high school but here she ran the celebration with the brisk tenderness of someone who had decided, years ago, that this park would have a Hanukkah whether anyone else scheduled one or not.

He found Alyvia and Benson at the table with the dreidels. Benson was spinning a dreidel he'd brought from home, an old wooden one his grandmother had given him, and it clattered against the plastic tabletop like a small argument. "You're on in a minute," Alyvia said. "She's doing the shammash families first." She pronounced it wrong, the way she pronounced everything in Hebrew wrong, with total confidence.

"They're not shammash families," Benjamin said. "There's only one shamash." He laid his candles on the table to count them, and this was where the trouble began, because Benson's dreidel knocked two of them into the gutter of the table and Benjamin, gathering them back, lost track of which he had counted. He counted again and got six. He counted again and got four. The candles looked exactly alike, thin white tapers with the same slight wobble at the base, as though even they couldn't tell themselves apart.

"Just take a handful," Benson said. "Extra candles, that's not a problem anyone in history has had."

"It is if I put up the wrong number." The menorah had nine branches, Benjamin knew that much, eight for the eight nights and the ninth for the shamash, the helper candle that lit all the others, one more each night. So tonight the thing should hold five candles total. He said this out loud, slowly, mostly to himself, and Alyvia said, "One more each night," as though confirming a password, and something in the glacial slowness of his own understanding irritated him, that he'd known the fact since he was seven and only now stood in the cold actually counting it.

The trouble underneath was not candles. The trouble was that his father's brother had died in the spring, and his uncle had been the one who lit the menorah every year at this park, humming off-key, holding the shamash at an angle no rabbi would endorse, and this year the family had agreed without discussing it that Benjamin would do it. Nobody had asked him. Nobody had to. His mother had simply handed him the candles the way you hand someone a coat, and he had put his arms through the sleeves.

Ms. López called his family's name. He took five candles, certain now, and climbed the bandstand steps where his parents stood at the menorah's base, his father holding a lighter he didn't seem to know what to do with. Benjamin fitted the candles into four of the holders and set the shamash in its branch, the one set apart, and his father lit the helper and passed it to him, and the flame traveled with a small wind-whipped sound like breath. His hand paused at the first candle. His uncle would have made a joke here, something about the oil lasting longer than anyone's patience, and the silence where the joke should be was so specific it was almost a sound of its own.

"You're allowed to take your time," his father said quietly, in the tone of a man who was also talking to himself.

Benjamin lit the first candle, then the second, the third, the fourth, and stood there with the shamash still burning in his fingers, holding the helper a moment longer than he needed to, because for eight nights this same candle would give itself away to light the others and tonight, at least, he understood that as something other than arithmetic. Below the bandstand, Alyvia was waving at him with both hands. Benson had stopped spinning his dreidel. The little flames bent sideways in the wind, straightened, and held, and Benjamin, still uncertain what he was to his family now, carried the shamash back to its branch and set it down still lit.
