fact: The InVID-WeVerify browser plugin, built by a European Union-funded project, splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched.
story:
Peyton had the video open on her phone for the third time when Avery found her at the back computers of the public library. On the screen, a flooded street, people wading past a submerged bus, a caption in bold letters: THIS IS HAPPENING NOW. SHARE. Eleven thousand shares already, and climbing.

"Camron posted it an hour ago," Avery said, dropping into the chair beside her. "Half the graduating class has it up. His cousin goes to that school district."

"That's the thing," Peyton said. "I don't know if it's that district."

Avery pulled her ponytail tight, a gesture Peyton had watched before every exam. "The bus says it. You can see the route number."

Peyton scrolled the comments. Prayers. Offers of blankets. Someone claiming to have donated two hundred dollars to a shelter that, as far as she could tell, did not exist. There was something in the whole assembly that felt staged, though she couldn't have said what, the way a too-neat omen can portend nothing at all.

She had been here before, in a different sense. Last spring her mother had brought her to the office on a snow day, and a colleague named Dirk had caught her scrolling her phone at the empty desk beside his. "Before you share anything," he had said, spinning his monitor toward her, "run it through this." He had clicked a button on a plugin in his browser, and a video on his screen had broken apart into a grid of still images, each one clickable. "It's called InVID-WeVerify," he had said. "Some European Union-funded project built it. It splits a video into key frames." He had dragged one of the frames into an image search and, two minutes later, found the same footage beneath a headline from four years ago and an ocean away. Peyton had laughed at the time, said something about how nobody she knew fell for that stuff, and Dirk had only shrugged and gone back to his spreadsheets.

She had not thought about it since. Now she opened the library computer's browser, found the plugin in the store, and installed it with the kind of quiet urgency that made Avery stop chewing her gum.

"What are you doing?"

"Something I saw once." She pasted the video's link. The plugin did what she remembered, splitting the clip into key frames, and she right-clicked the clearest one, the flooded bus, and sent it out to the image search.

The results loaded slowly. The library's wifi was its usual self. Avery leaned in, and behind them a toddler shrieked somewhere near the picture books, and Mr. Aydın, the librarian, passed by with a cart and paused, looking over their shoulders with the mild entitlement of someone who had watched a decade of teenagers discover things at these terminals.

The first match was a news article. Not this district, not even this country. The flood was real, the water and the wading people were real, but the article was dated two years back, and the caption on Peyton's phone said NOW. She scrolled further. A second article, then a third, same frames, same bus.

"Send it to Camron," Avery said, already typing on her own phone.

"No." Peyton closed the search window and then opened it again, because closing it felt like hiding it. "He'll just say I'm calling him a liar."

"You're not calling him anything. You're showing him where it's from."

But Peyton sat still, her hands flat on the desk. She thought about how she had wanted it to be true, in the strange way people want a disaster to belong to them, to be able to say they had been close to it, that their school, their river, their town. Two years ago she would have shared it in a heartbeat. Even now some part of her hesitated, and she was honest enough to admit that the hesitation wasn't about Camron's feelings. It was about preferring the version where the flood was happening now, where her outrage was useful, where she could be one of the good ones passing along the alarm.

"There's still a flood in those articles," she said finally. "Just not ours. Those people were real too." It sounded weaker than she meant it. She thought of her history teacher's word for the study of how stories get written and rewritten, how the same event becomes different facts depending on who found the frame first. Historiography, he had called it, and she had rolled her eyes at the term all year.

She took a screenshot of the search results and sent it to Camron with no caption, then set the phone face-down on the desk. Whether he took it down, whether he argued, whether the shares kept climbing with the borrowed water and the borrowed grief, she couldn't control. Avery was still typing beside her. The toddler shrieked again. Mr. Aydín slid a scrap of paper across the desk, and on it he had written, in librarian's pencil, one more search term to try.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Programmers describe linear search as O(n), meaning its work grows in step with the list, and binary search as O(log n), meaning its work grows with the logarithm of the list's size.
story:
The whiteboard in Cabin C smelled of stale marker and lake water, and someone had written O(log n) across it in letters the size of dinner plates. Violet stood in front of it with her elbows out, guarding the markers the way a dragon guards gold, because Jace kept trying to steal them to draw a shark.

"Explain it," said Ms. Zhou from the doorway. She had a clipboard, a whistle, and the unhurried manner of someone who had spent the morning rescuing canoes. "Before the group votes on which search we use for the roster app. That scribble is yours, I assume."

"It's mine," Violet said. She had written it at two in the morning, when the cicadas outside had finally quieted enough for her to think. The camp's roster app needed to look up campers by ID number, and the IDs were sorted, and half the cabin had been arguing about whether it mattered.

"So the roster has four hundred campers," Oceanne said, perched on the picnic table someone had dragged indoors. "If we go down the list one at a time, is that the linear search?"

"That's linear," Violet said. "Programmers call it O(n). The work grows in step with the list. Double the campers, double the work."

Jace raised his marker like a scepter. "And I say that's fine. Four hundred names is nothing. My phone has a trillion photos of Oceanne's dog."

"He does," Oceanne confirmed. "It's penurious with storage for everything except my dog."

"That's not what penurious means," Violet said. "It means stingy. Cheap."

"His phone is stingy," Jace said. "It deletes my screenshots and keeps the dog."

Ms. Zhou tapped her clipboard once, which was her way of saying get back to it, and Violet turned to the board. She drew a long rectangle and cut it in half with one stroke of the marker. "Binary search. The list is sorted, so you look at the middle, and you know which half the answer is in. Then you cut that half in half. The work grows with the logarithm of the list's size. That's the O(log n) on the board. Ten times as many campers is barely any more work."

"Say the number part again," Oceanne said. "Slower. I was thinking about the dog."

"The work grows with the logarithm of the list's size. Not in step with the list. With the log of it." Violet said it slowly and found, saying it, that she finally believed it herself. She had copied the idea from a forum post at two a.m. and had not been sure until this moment, marker squeaking, that she understood what she was claiming.

Jace put on a wounded voice. "So I'm the apologist for the slow search now. Defender of checking every single name like an honest person."

"You're the apologist for not thinking," Oceanne said. "Which, respect, is a full time job in your case."

"You cajoled me into this app in the first place," Jace said, pointing the marker at her. "You said it would take one afternoon. That was three days ago. There was weeping. Mine."

"There was light weeping," Ms. Zhou agreed, making a note on her clipboard that Violet very much hoped was not about the weeping.

"So here's what I actually think," Violet said, and everyone turned, which surprised her a little. "Binary search wins on a sorted list, that part's not close. But the roster isn't always sorted. When the registrar adds people at the end of the day, it's a mess until someone sorts it, and sorting costs work too. Linear doesn't care. It just walks the list." She capped the marker. "I don't know which one we should use until I see how bad the roster gets. I'm not going to pretend I do."

The cabin went quiet in the way it did when the loons started up across the lake, everyone listening to the wrong thing so they could avoid the right one. Then Ms. Zhou said, "Vote anyway. That's what engineers do, they vote and then they're wrong together."

They voted. It came out three to two for binary, Jace abstaining on the grounds that his marker was running dry and this was clearly a sign. Oceanne hugged the picnic table. Someone knocked over a thermos of bug spray, which is a sentence Violet would not have believed a week ago, and the smell of citronella rolled through the cabin like a slow green wave while everyone laughed and gagged at once.

After lights out she sat on the porch with the roster file open on her borrowed laptop, its screen the only light besides the moon on the water. She scrolled to the bottom of the list and found the newest camper, appended last, out of order, ID number standing there like a stranger at the wrong door. She looked at it for a long moment. Then she got out her notebook and wrote, at the top of a clean page, "sort how often?" and underlined it twice.

From inside the cabin Jace's voice floated out, muffled by a pillow. "Are you fixing the app or are you drawing my shark?"

"Both," Violet called back, and started drawing the fin.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: Automation bias is the tendency to favor suggestions from automated systems and to ignore contradicting information, even when that information is correct.
story:
The kitchen smelled of burnt garlic bread, and the clock over the stove read 8:14, which meant they had three hours and forty-six minutes to decide what to submit to the district's ethics competition before the portal closed at midnight. Megan set her laptop at the end of the table between the salad bowl and Mohamad's elbow, opened the draft titled "Early Warning: A Case Study," and waited for someone to say the thing nobody wanted to say.

"We could cut the part about you," Maxence said to Mohamad, not looking up from his phone. "Make it about a hypothetical student. The committee doesn't need a real name."

Mohamad tore a piece of bread in half and didn't eat either half. "The whole point is that it's real. The system flagged me because of my address and my bus route, not because I was failing. If we make it hypothetical, we're just instantiating the same problem. A made-up kid nobody has to answer for."

Megan's mother put down the pasta pot and said, perhaps unwisely, "But the school apologized, didn't they? It got fixed."

"It got fixed for him," Megan said. "The system didn't get fixed. Mr. Yang still teaches two flagged kids in third period." She heard her own voice go flat and made herself soften it. "That's the part they don't want in a district competition."

The doorbell rang. It was Mr. Yang, holding a casserole dish with a towel over it, on his way back from the school's evening conference and, as he put it, in need of witnesses to his cooking. Megan's mother made room; the table became crowded and warm, and Megan felt a presentiment, small and cold under all that warmth, that the evening was about to hand her something she would have to carry.

Mr. Yang sat down, tasted the pasta, approved of it, and then, while Mohamad ladled sauce, mentioned his wife. She had driven to the conference through the hills, he said, and the GPS had taken her down Hollow Creek Road, which was closed for repaving, barriers up and everything, orange signs in plain view. She'd eased around the barrier. A neighbor had called the county about it before, apparently; other drivers did the same thing every week. The tow truck came within the hour, at least.

Maxence laughed, then stopped. "Wait. There's a name for that. We read it for psych. It's called automation bias." He was already scrolling, and he turned the screen so Mohamad could see. "People favor what the automated system tells them and ignore contradicting information, even when that information is correct."

"It's just a GPS," Megan's mother said.

Megan looked at the draft glowing at the end of the table, at the section titled "Findings," and felt the floor of the argument shift. She had written eight pages about bias in the training data, about what the model had learned from old attendance records, and she had left out the more disturbing half. The signs had been there in Mohamad's case too. His grades were posted on the same portal as the flag. Two teachers had clicked past the warning, past the A-minus average, past the note from his counselor, and scheduled the intervention meeting anyway, because the system had told them to. The contradiction was correct, and they had driven around the barrier.

"Here's the problem," she said slowly. "We've been writing about a biased machine. But Mr. Yang's wife's GPS wasn't biased. It was just out of date. What made the tow truck necessary was her. What made Mohamad's meeting happen was the teachers. The machine said jump and they jumped, and the signs saying don't jump were right there." She pulled the laptop toward her. "The report is about the wrong thing. Or half the wrong thing."

"The portal closes at midnight," Maxence said. "We can't rewrite the thesis in three hours."

"You can cut mine out in three seconds," Mohamad said, and there it was, the subtext surfacing at last: he had never actually agreed to be the case study, had let them talk him into it in the library because they'd been excited, because they'd said his story would instantiate the argument better than statistics. His fork was set down parallel to his plate, his bread untouched, and Megan understood that what she'd been calling his story had been his file, opened at a dinner table with a teacher sitting three feet away.

Mr. Yang, who had been quiet through all of this, said only, "The conference packet had my flagged kids in it too. Third period. I signed the attendance sheet without reading theirs." He said it to his casserole, not to anyone.

Megan closed the laptop lid halfway, then opened it again. "New plan," she said. "It's your name or no name, your call, and if it's no name we submit what we can honestly say by midnight, even if it's shorter and worse and doesn't win anything." She turned the screen toward Mohamad and slid the keyboard across the tablecloth, past the salad bowl, and waited.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: False friends are words that look alike in two languages but differ in meaning; Spanish 'embarazada' means pregnant, not embarrassed.
story:
The restaurant had cleared its tables to one side for the debate club, and Rose stood near the kitchen door with her note cards sweating in her hand. The topic was immigration policy, and she had drawn the affirmative side, and she had five minutes to argue it entirely in Spanish while Mr. Lawson timed her from the counter with his phone raised like a verdict.

"You've got this," Cameron said, sliding a water glass across the table toward her. "You drilled those phrases all week."

"Then why can't I feel my hands," Rose said.

Keegan, who had drawn the negative and would speak after her, was leaning back in his chair with his own cards fanned out, unhurried, already performing calm. That was the thing about Keegan: his ease made everyone else's nerves look like an admission of weakness. Rose watched him and decided not to match it. Let him be smooth. She would be prepared.

Mr. Lawson called her name. The leftover diners, a few parents, and the whole Advanced Spanish class turned toward the front, and the dim room with its hanging lamps and its little igneous paperweights anchoring the tablecloths seemed to arrange itself around her. She began. Her opening was better than she'd feared; the argument about labor markets came out in whole, connected sentences. Then, reaching for the word to describe politicians who were embarrassed by their own hypocrisy, she said "avergonzado," lost the thread of the gender agreement, panicked, and reached instead for a word that had always felt safer because it looked like the English one. "Los políticos están muy embarazados," she said.

The Advanced Spanish class laughed. Not a ripple, a real laugh, heads tipping back. Rose stood in it without understanding, and her face went hot, and Mr. Lawson's timer thumb did not move.

"False friends," Keegan said softly from his chair, not unkindly, the way you'd identify a species of bird. "Embarazada means pregnant, not embarrassed."

Rose looked at him. The laughter was still settling, and inside it she turned the sentence over. She had known this once, she was almost sure, from some worksheet in September, filed and forgotten. Now the room had taught it to her with its whole body. She let the silence stretch one second longer than was comfortable, then said, in Spanish, "Perhaps the politicians are pregnant with promises they will never deliver." It was a save, and a cheap one, and she heard the class decide to laugh again, this time with her.

She used the rest of her five minutes differently than she had planned. She had come in arguing that the economic case for open labor markets was decisive, that the numbers settled it. Standing there with her notes half useless, she found herself saying instead that the numbers and the human claims pointed the same direction but did not prove each other, that she believed the policy was right partly because of the data and partly because of something the data could not reach, and that she could not fully separate the two even if she wanted to seem rigorous. Mr. Lawson's thumb came down. Keegan took the floor, and his rebuttal was fluent and merciless, and Rose watched him mesmerize the room the way he always did, effortless, his Spanish folding over hers like a nicer suit.

But she noticed, in the last of his five minutes, that he kept both sides of the argument clean and separate, the economics here, the ethics there, nothing touching, and she thought that tidiness might be its own kind of dodge. She wasn't sure. She was still not sure when Mr. Lawson collected the ballots and the class crowded toward the counter to order food, and Keegan came over to her table carrying two glasses of horchata and set one down in front of her.

"That comeback," he said. "The pregnant promises. Mr. Lawson wrote something down right after."

"Was it a point for me or a note about my pedantry?"

"Yours, definitely. Mine's the pedantry." He lifted his glass. "To false friends."

They drank. Behind him, Mr. Lawson was reading the ballots at the counter, his pen moving down the page, and Rose could not tell from his face whether he was tallying or just correcting.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear.
story:
Michael's mother had left the recipe card on the counter beside two onions and a bag of carrots, and when she called from work to ask if he would handle dinner, he acceded before he had fully decided to. The soup was her mother's, written in faded ink on an index card so old it felt obsolescent, a relic from a time when recipes traveled by hand instead of phone. It was a warm evening, so he carried the cutting board and the pot out to the backyard table, where the light lasted longer and the grill, which nobody had used in years, stood rusting quietly by the fence like a retired relative.

He was arranging the carrots when his sister came out and sat down across from him. She had been strange all week, quiet at meals, disappearing into her room, and their father had taken to knocking on her door with the careful manner of a man defusing something. Now she picked up the paring knife without being asked and began peeling the onions, and Michael, wary of disturbing whatever was in her, said nothing and let her work.

Within a minute her eyes were streaming. She wiped them with the heel of her hand, an old mannerism of hers, the wrist dragged across the face, and then she was blinking hard and laughing a little at herself, and Michael, relieved to have something ordinary to say, teased her. "You're crying over an onion. That's pathetic." She threw a piece of peel at him. Thomas and Ricardo arrived halfway through, drawn by the promise of food, and Thomas picked up the teasing where Michael had left it, asking whether she needed a moment, whether they should give her some privacy to grieve.

"Go look it up," she said, and shoved her phone across the table at him. Thomas typed, held the screen close to his face, and read aloud. "Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear." He pronounced it slowly, syllable by syllable, and Ricardo tried to repeat it and failed, mangling it into something that made even the sister laugh through her wet lashes.

Michael took the phone and read the passage again himself, feeling something shift in his understanding, small but real. He had assumed, walking out the door earlier, that his sister was crying about the thing she had been refusing to talk about, some disappointment or fear he had guessed at and not named. He had been gentler with her all week for it, holding doors, offering the good chair, the way you soften around grief. Now he sat with the unglamorous chemistry of it and had to admit that the tears on her face might mean nothing more than a vapor finding her eyes.

But only might. He considered the two ideas side by side, the way he was learning to do with arguments in his English class, testing each against what he actually knew. The tears were onions. The silence at dinner was something else. Both could be true in the same girl on the same evening, and the onion did not disprove the sadness, any more than the sadness had caused the tears. He could not tell where one ended and the other began, and he suspected he was not supposed to be able to.

He chopped the second onion himself, deliberately, watching the water rise in his own eyes and learning from the inside what a body could do without permission from the heart. Ricardo handed him the carrots. Thomas fetched bowls from the kitchen without being asked, which surprised everyone, and Mr. Chatterjee appeared at the fence in his gardening gloves, sniffed the air, and said the smell reminded him of a soup his own mother used to make, before he had known enough English to read a recipe card.

They ladled it out at the backyard table as the sky went violet, and it was good, better than Michael had expected, and his sister ate two bowls and said their grandmother would have been proud. Michael wanted to ask her then, quietly, about the week, but she was mopping the last of the broth with bread, and he decided the soup had already said most of what he knew how to say. He reached over and took her empty bowl before she could rise with it.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Most of Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights, published in 1847, is told by the housekeeper Nelly Dean to the visitor Lockwood, so events reach readers through two narrators with their own biases.
story:
Blake had read the chapter twice and still couldn't tell whether Heathcliff was a monster or whether someone wanted him to look like one. He spread the novel flat on the library table, spine cracking softly, and stared at the page as if the type itself might rearrange under enough pressure.

"You're doing the face," Jaden said, dropping into the chair across from him with a milk carton he wasn't supposed to have in here. "The face you do before you decide the assignment is stupid."

"It's not stupid. It's the opposite of stupid, that's the problem." Blake turned the book so Jaden could see. "Everything we know about these people, we get secondhand. There's this guy Lockwood, a visitor, and he's basically writing down what the housekeeper tells him. Nelly Dean. She saw most of it, or says she did."

Imane arrived with her laptop already open, sliding in beside Jaden. She wanted the essay done before Friday so she could spend the weekend at her sister's recital, and she had a system: split the chapter, swap notes, five-paragraph structure, done. "Okay, so Nelly's the narrator. Unreliable narrators lie or exaggerate. We find three examples, we write it up. There's a template for this."

"Three examples of what, though?" Blake asked. "She doesn't exactly lie. That's what's bugging me. Lying would be easier."

Ms. Chowdhury passed their table on her way to the returns cart, paused long enough to read the title upside down, and said only, "Brontë makes you work for it," before moving on, which Blake found both unhelpful and somehow encouraging.

He started flipping back through the early chapters, hunting for the moments where Nelly's own opinions leaked in. He'd highlighted one already, a place where Nelly called Heathcliff a demon of a child, and now he noticed the words around it: how Nelly admitted she'd neglected him, slighted him, favored Hindley. He'd read past that the first time. He read it again, slower.

"Wait," he said. "Listen to this part." He read the passage aloud, the one where Nelly confesses she treated the boy badly when he arrived. "So she's telling us she was unfair to him. And then every time she describes him after that, she's describing someone she had a grudge against. She's not lying. She's just... colored."

Imane stopped typing. "You're saying her dislike changes the story."

"I'm saying I can't get at the story at all. Everything reaches us through her, and through Lockwood, and neither of them is neutral. It's like, I don't know, symbiosis. The story can't exist without them, but they're feeding on it too, shaping it to fit what they already believe." He winced at himself. "That sounded like a fortune cookie."

"It kind of worked though," Jaden said, spinning the milk carton on its corner. "So which one do we trust? That's the essay, right?"

"That's what I don't know yet." Blake drew a line down his notebook page and wrote NELLY on one side and LOCKWOOD on the other. "Maybe neither. Maybe that's the whole point, that we can't abrogate our judgment to either of them. We have to decide for ourselves what actually happened." He looked at the two columns, empty except for the names, and felt the small vertigo of a question that didn't come with an answer key. Outside the tall windows the afternoon had gone gray, the light boreal and thin, like something from another latitude had drifted in over the parking lot.

Imane pulled the book toward herself and found the passage he'd read, running her finger under the lines. "Okay," she said slowly, "but if we can't trust her, then we can't trust that she was unfair to him either. She might be making herself look better with a fake confession."

Blake sat back. He hadn't thought of that. The fake confession, the unreliable narrator admitting to a small cruelty to hide a larger one, or maybe genuinely confessing, or maybe nothing at all. He wrote a question mark between the two columns.

"So what do we write?" Jaden asked.

Blake capped his pen and looked at the two of them. "We write the question."

"Ms. Chowdhury's going to love that," Imane said, but she was already deleting her template.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many Orthodox churches, including the Russian Orthodox Church, celebrate Christmas on January 7 because they keep December 25 on the older Julian calendar.
story:
Sarah's grandmother had pressed the pin into her palm outside the community hall, a small enamel star, and said, "Wear it tonight, so you remember what day it is." That had been three hours ago, and Sarah still wasn't sure what day it was. Inside, the hall smelled of wax and fried dough, and a table of older women was laying out kutia in blue-rimmed bowls while her grandfather argued cheerfully with Mr. Grewal about where the extension cords should run.

"It's the seventh of January," her grandfather announced to no one in particular, "and it is Christmas. Truly Christmas. Not the one the neighbors had."

Sarah had known this, sort of, all her life, the way she knew the words to songs in a language she couldn't really speak. But this year was the first year she'd had to explain it out loud, to Armaan and Delphine at school, and she'd done it badly. "We do Christmas later," she'd said, which made it sound like a scheduling error, a family that couldn't get organized in time. Delphine had laughed, not unkindly, and Armaan had asked if she got double presents, and Sarah had laughed too, and then hated herself a little for the laugh, because the answer was no, and the reason was not nothing.

The reason sat in the front pew of the temporary icon corner they'd set up by the stage, where her grandmother was adjusting a cloth. Later, when Sarah asked her properly, in the kitchen behind the hall, her grandmother said it plainly while stirring poppy seed filling. "Our church keeps the old calendar. December 25, but on the Julian one, so it lands here, on January 7." She tapped the spoon on the pot's rim. "Your mother's people have the twenty-fifth of the Gregorian. Same feast. Different arithmetic." She said it without apology, the way she said most things, as though the fact were a chair you could either sit in or trip over.

Sarah's mother had married out, as the aunts put it, and the family had spent fifteen years performing a truce over it. Every January her mother came to this dinner, and every year she sat slightly forward, ready to leave, and Sarah had spent years reading that posture as judgment. It had been easier to think her mother was impatient with all of it than to think harder about what patience would actually look like. Tonight, watching her mother help Grandmother carry the trays, Sarah found she had to revise something, and revising it felt less like a decision than like water finding a lower place.

Earlier in the evening there had been a collection jar by the door, marked for a family on their street whose apartment had burned in November. Mr. Grewal, who ran the hall bookings, had matched whatever came in, and he stood near the jar now, counting quietly. Sarah overheard him tell Armaan, who had come after all, surprising her, that he did it because he remembered being new to this country and nearly destitute, sleeping in the back of his cousin's shop. "It wasn't happenstance that somebody fed me," he said. "It was a woman from a church like this one. So now I stand here." Armaan put in five dollars, and then, visibly recalculating his weekend, another five.

The choir began, four men and a boy, and the sound they made undulated through the hall, low then lower, so that the conversations at the back dimmed without anyone deciding to quiet them. Delphine leaned toward Sarah and whispered, "So this is real Christmas? Like, actually Christmas?" and Sarah opened her mouth to give the easy answer, the one about doing it later, and closed it again. "It's Christmas on the old calendar," she said. "December 25, the Julian way, which puts it on January 7." Delphine nodded slowly, the way people do when a fact rearranges furniture in their heads, and said, "Huh. So the neighbors' trees are already at the curb and you're just starting."

There was a moment, later, when Sarah stood with her grandmother near the icon corner, both of them holding cups of tea that neither was drinking, and her grandmother said, without looking at her, "You laughed at school. When they asked you." Sarah felt the heat climb her neck. "How do you know that?" "Armaan tells me things. He thinks I don't remember his name, but I do." Grandmother sipped. "I laughed too, at your age. At everything. It is a way of carrying something without carrying it." She set the cup down. "I am not telling you it was wrong. I am telling you I did it too, and it didn't protect me from anything."

Sarah turned that over while the night wound down, chairs stacking, the boy soprano being hugged by all four men in turn, her mother and grandmother standing close enough that their shoulders touched, neither one yielding and neither one stepping back. She thought about the two calendars laid over each other like transparencies, the same star seen through two sheets of glass, and she understood that she could hold both her grandmother's arithmetic and her mother's without choosing, and she also understood that she couldn't prove the holding would hold, that some years it might all slide, that she was eighteen and making a promise she didn't yet know the terms of. Mr. Grewal was rolling up the cord by the door. She went to help him, and he handed her one end, and together they walked it in, loop by loop, until the last of it coiled quiet in his hands.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The 26th Amendment, which set the US voting age at 18, was ratified in 1971 in about three months, faster than any other amendment.
story:
The meatloaf was half gone before Kevin slid the sample ballot from his back pocket and unfolded it on the table, between the mashed potatoes and his father's elbow. "Election's Tuesday," he said. "I'm registered at the library branch on Miller."

His grandmother reached over and pressed the paper flat with two fingers, tilting her head at the rows of names. "Eighteen and voting. I was married before I could vote."

Kevin looked up. "What do you mean, you couldn't vote?"

"The voting age was twenty-one back then. I turned eighteen in 1969." She picked up her fork, then set it down again. "You'd have thought a girl old enough to work, old enough to be a wife, would count. Not for that."

"But eighteen's, like, the whole thing." He turned the ballot over as if the rule might be printed on the back. "It's just how it is."

"They changed it while I was in college," she said. "The 26th Amendment. Set the voting age at eighteen. Ratified in 1971, and it went through in about three months." She smiled at his face. "Faster than any other amendment. We used to say the country could move when it wanted to."

Kevin's father snorted from the head of the table. "It'll be slower going backward, I can promise you that." He said it lightly, but nobody laughed, and his eyes stayed on his plate.

That night Kevin sat on his bed with his phone and read until the screen dimmed against his thumb. Farhan had texted him a vitriolic thread about one of the school board candidates, all caps and exclamation points, calling her a parasite who wanted to gut the arts program. Sirine had sent the same candidate's endorsement page, teachers he recognized, Ms. Paquette's name third from the top. Ms. Paquette, who had stayed late every Thursday to run the lit magazine, who had told him his essay on his grandfather was the best thing a senior had handed her in nine years. Farhan's thread had twenty screenshots. Sirine had sent one link and the words "make up your own mind."

He read both. Then he read the candidate's own words, then the minutes of the board meeting where she'd voted against the theater renovation, then the follow-up where she explained the vote, and the explanation was not what Farhan's screenshots said it was, and also not nothing. It was a budget argument with people on both sides of it who taught kids he knew.

At dinner the next evening his father asked, "Decided yet?"

"Mostly." Kevin reached for the bread. "Farhan thinks anyone who votes for Carlson is a coward. Sirine thinks anyone who votes against her is ignorant. They're both being stupid about it."

"That's my boy," his father said. "Split the difference."

"I'm not splitting the difference." He heard how sharp it came out and lowered his voice. "I read her actual voting record. The theater thing was bad. But she wrote the grant that kept the tutoring center open, and Farhan used that center for two years and doesn't know it." He tore the bread in half and didn't eat either piece. "I'm voting for her, and I think the theater vote was wrong, and I don't know how both of those fit in one person. I'm not pretending they do."

His grandmother watched him across the table. "When the amendment passed, my father said one vote wouldn't matter. I went anyway. Stood in a gymnasium in a line that barely moved." She paused. "It was the first time anyone official had ever asked me what I thought."

Tuesday morning Kevin woke before his alarm. The library branch smelled like floor wax and old paper, and a woman with a clipboard found his name in the binder and pointed him to booth four. The pen was chained to the shelf. He filled in the circle for the school board, then the county judge, then worked down to the state question he'd changed his mind about three times since Sunday and filled in that one too, his hand steady even though the rest of him wasn't sure.

He fed the ballot into the machine, and it made a small mechanical sound, like a stamp, like something being sealed. Outside, Farhan was leaning against the bike rack.

"Well?" Farhan said. "Tell me you didn't."

Kevin zipped his jacket. "Get in line," he said. "It's your turn."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it.
story:
Kyle had promised Bodhi the model would be finished by Friday, and by Thursday night it was still only half painted, sitting between the salt shaker and his mother's unfinished crossword at the kitchen table. It was a ruined chapel for their history diorama, gray stone walls and a slate roof, and the deadline felt interminable and then suddenly near, the way deadlines do. He mixed his gray from black and white in a jar lid, tested it on a scrap of foam, and started on the east wall.

Bodhi had done the figures, the tiny soldiers whose tunics were a deep orange he'd insisted on, some argument about the regiment's actual colors. Kyle set two of them on the chapel steps to see how the scene looked, and that was when he noticed it. The gray wall behind the orange soldiers seemed almost blue, faintly cold, while the same gray on the far wall, the one he'd painted before dinner, looked brownish, warm, like wet clay. He leaned close. It was the same paint. He had stirred it himself.

He brought the two soldiers to the other wall and set them there, on a flat stone he'd made from the same gray. The wall behind them cooled again. When he moved them away it warmed. He got his phone and took a photo, then a photo of the jar lid, then a photo with his thumb covering half the frame, as if the camera might catch his eyes lying to him.

Rhys would have said he was overthinking it. Rhys, who had told the whole class that the diorama was a waste of a weekend, was its loudest detractor, mostly, Kyle suspected, because nobody had asked him to help. Kyle texted him a photo of the two walls anyway, captioned "same gray, right?" and got back a thumbs down and the word lighting. But the kitchen light was the same over both walls. He stood a pencil upright between them to be sure it cast only one shadow.

It was Ms. Johansson's class that had them doing the diorama, and he thought about texting her, then didn't, because she had a way of answering questions with questions that he was not in the mood for at ten at night. Instead he searched "gray looks different colors next to orange" and started scrolling. Most of it was junk. Then he found a page about a chemist, Michel Eugène Chevreul, who had published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. He read the sentence twice. Complement: orange on one side, blue across from it. That was why his gray went cold behind the soldiers.

He had been inured to small failures in this project, hours spent carving doors that split, glue on his jeans, so the discovery felt almost illicit, like cheating on a test he'd been failing. He painted a stripe of the gray on a scrap, laid orange paper beside half of it, and watched the unpainted half of the stripe turn faintly, undeniably bluer. Not the paint. His eyes. Or not only his eyes; the page said the color appears to shift, and he liked the word appears, which left room for the strangeness of it, the fact that a thing could be true and not be true at the same time, depending on what stood beside it.

The problem was what to do about it. If he kept the orange soldiers on the steps, the east wall would read cold and the rest of the chapel warm, and Bodhi would notice, or worse, wouldn't, and the whole thing would look accidental. He could glaze the east wall with a thin brown wash to correct it. Or he could leave it, even push it, keep the soldiers clustered so that one wall of the chapel stood in a kind of blue shadow the stone itself never earned. He sat with his brush hovering, and understood that he couldn't know which was right until it was done and too late to undo.

Rhys replied eventually, past eleven: it's the photo, phones do that. Kyle didn't argue. He had the scrap of gray on the table in front of him, half of it still lying against the orange paper, and that wasn't a phone. But he also knew that saying so would mean an argument, and tomorrow they would all be in the same classroom looking at the same chapel, and either it would work or it wouldn't.

He thinned some brown with water until it was barely a color, more of a suspicion, and touched it to the east wall in a single small stroke, low down, where the shadow of the steps would fall. He stepped back to the doorway and looked. Then he picked the smallest soldier off the scrap and set him at the base of the wall, right beside it.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In England and Wales, a landlord must place a tenant's deposit in a government-backed protection scheme within 30 days of receiving it.
story:
Nikola's message arrived while Jordyn was still on the train, somewhere past the border into Wales. He had signed for a flat in Cardiff three weeks ago, he said, handed over five weeks of rent as a deposit, and never received a single piece of paperwork about it. He asked if that was normal. Jordyn read it twice, then put the phone face-down on her knees and watched the fields go slate-grey and then actual slate, stacked in walls like rows of broken teeth.

Her grandmother's house sat at the end of a lane where the hedges grew so high the sky seemed to be rationed. Jordyn came every August, partly because she was expected to and partly because the house had a stillness her own home lacked, a quality she thought of as igneous, something cooled and solidified ages ago and now impossible to crack. Her grandmother met her at the gate with flour on her hands. They ate seedcake. They argued mildly about politics, as they always did; her grandmother had voted in some local plebiscite about a bypass and still felt betrayed by the outcome. It was, Jordyn thought, the safest argument they had.

The second message came that evening. Nikola again. He had asked his landlord's agent for the deposit certificate and been told to stop being difficult. Jordyn sat on the window seat with her phone, drafting replies she deleted. She knew almost nothing about renting. Her parents talked about their mortgage the way other families talked about weather, a permanent low-pressure system of interest and repayments, and she'd absorbed only the shape of it: that you borrowed an enormous sum, that the house stood as collateral, that after twenty-five years you were supposed to own it outright. Renting, to her, had always been the thing other people did, the version without the ending. She had never once wondered where a deposit actually went after you handed it over.

She went downstairs to look for her grandmother and found the study door open and the desk lamp on. Her grandmother was going through a drawer of papers, and on top of the pile was a tenancy agreement. The name on it stopped Jordyn in the doorway. It was Nikola's, his looping signature, the address in Cardiff. The date was three weeks old.

"You're his landlord," Jordyn said.

Her grandmother took off her glasses. She said it had seemed sensible, the flat above the old chemist's, an investment now that the pension was what it was. She said the agent handled everything. When Jordyn asked, slowly, what the agent had done with the deposit, her grandmother said, with a small frown, that it had gone into her account, of course, where else would it go, and it would come back to the boy when he left, less any damages.

Jordyn felt the situation catalyze into something she couldn't smooth over with politeness. She asked if she could use the computer, and in the study, with her grandmother reading over her shoulder, she typed the question Nikola had asked her. Within minutes she had it. In England and Wales, a landlord had to place a tenant's deposit in a government-backed protection scheme within 30 days of receiving it. She read the line aloud. Thirty days. Not a suggestion, not a courtesy. She counted backward on her fingers and found that nineteen of them were already gone.

Her grandmother said the agent had never mentioned any scheme. Then she said, more quietly, that perhaps the agent had kept the money himself, and Jordyn watched her straighten the papers as though tidiness could undo the arithmetic. The two versions of the problem sat side by side in Jordyn's head: her grandmother had not known, which was forgivable; the agent may have taken the money, which was not; and Nikola was sleeping above a chemist's shop in Cardiff with his savings sitting in the wrong account, trusting people because he had no better option. She could not make these fit together, and she did not pretend to.

She picked up her phone and started typing to Nikola, then stopped, thumb hovering, because whatever she sent would either set him against her grandmother or leave him uninformed, and she could not yet tell which was the kinder cruelty. Eleven days remained. That much, at least, was still true.

"Call the agent," Jordyn said. "Tonight. Before you decide what to tell him."

Her grandmother reached for the phone on the desk, and her hand was not quite steady.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: An adjustable-rate mortgage's interest rate changes periodically with a market index, so its monthly payment can rise, unlike a fixed-rate mortgage's.
story:
Violet waited in the molded plastic chair by the teller windows while her mother stood at a desk across the lobby, signing a stack of papers that kept getting taller. The bank smelled of carpet cleaner and warm toner, and a space heater near the door rattled whenever the automatic glass slid open. She had come because the apartment above Mr. Li's shop had a For Rent sign in the window, and her mother had said, "You should see this part," without explaining which part.

The loan officer, a woman with reading glasses pushed up into her hair, slid one page toward her mother and tapped a number near the bottom. "This is the new payment amount, effective next month."

"But nothing changed," her mother said. "Same house, same bank, same everything."

The woman turned the page around so Violet, leaning over, could see the columns. "Your rate adjusts with the market index. It's an adjustable-rate mortgage. That's what the A in ARM stands for. The payment can go up, unlike a fixed-rate mortgage, where it never does."

Her mother's pen hovered above the signature line without descending.

Brock from school walked in with his father, carrying a shoebox of quarters for the coin counter, and did a double take when he saw Violet. He mouthed something she couldn't parse, then transliterated it slowly, letter by letter, with exaggerated lips: H-O-W L-O-N-G. She held up two fingers and shrugged. He and his father took a number and sat three chairs down, and Brock started stacking quarters into towers on his knee while his father read a brochure about certificates of deposit with the concentration of a man avoiding something.

"The rent on Mr. Li's place," Violet said quietly, when her mother sat down beside her while the loan officer photocopied something. "How is it different from this?"

"Rent is what you pay to live in someone else's place. A mortgage is you buying a place, borrowing the money to do it, paying it back over years." Her mother rubbed the crease between her eyebrows. "Mr. Li owns that building. His mortgage on it might be fixed or adjustable, same as ours. If his payment went up, our rent might go up too."

"Even though the apartment didn't change."

"Even though."

Violet thought of Lily, who had spent all of junior year calling landlords parasitism with a human face, and of Mr. Li, who had once replaced the hinge on their mailbox for free and refused the twenty-dollar bill her mother tried to press into his hand. Lily's word and Mr. Li's hinge were both true at once, and she couldn't make them collapse into one thing, and she was tired of pretending she had to pick. The feeling was inchoate, less a position than a pressure, so she decided to do what she did in chemistry: get data.

She crossed the lobby while her mother was still signing and found Brock at the coin counter, feeding quarters into the slot with the patience of someone feeding a goat. "Your dad rent or own?"

"Rent." A quarter dropped. "He's saving a down payment. That's the chunk you pay up front so the bank trusts you for the rest. He's got this jar at home, it's disgusting, it's like forty pounds of change."

"So rent goes to the landlord forever, and a down payment goes toward actually owning."

"Depends if the landlord's honest." Another quarter. "Mr. Li puts our rent receipts in a ledger with a fountain pen. My dad says he's the last of a kind."

When Violet came back, her mother was at the teller window making a deposit, sliding a check through the slot, and the teller counted the balance back to her in a low voice. Outside, the sky had gone the color of a bruise over the pharmacy sign, and Mr. Li's shop two doors down had its lights on, the For Rent sign glowing faintly orange in the window.

Her mother pocketed the receipt. "New payment starts the first of the month. We'll manage."

"Can we go see the apartment before someone else takes it?"

"You want to move above the shop?"

"I want to see what four hundred more a month buys us, or doesn't." Violet pulled her jacket zipper up. "And I want to ask Mr. Li one question first."

They pushed through the doors into the cold. Inside the shop, Mr. Li was wrapping a newspaper around a jar of something, and he looked up at the bell.

"Mr. Li," Violet said. "Your mortgage on the building. Fixed or adjustable?"

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
story:
Eli had read the article twice on Tuesday and once more in the parking lot of the coffee shop before he turned off his phone and put it in the glovebox, where it could not tempt him. The article had said that in 1997 a researcher named Arthur Aron had paired up strangers and had them take turns asking each other thirty-six questions that grew gradually more personal, and that afterward those pairs felt closer than pairs who had only made small talk. He was not sure he believed it. But it was the only plan he had.

His date's name was Gillian. They had met in the hallway outside Mr. Karimi's classroom, where they had both been waiting to argue about a grade, and the argument had turned into laughing, and the laughing had turned into this: seven o'clock, a table by the window, two cups going cold.

The small talk lasted eleven minutes. He counted them on the clock above the pastry case. The town, the weather, whether the coffee here was better than the coffee at the other place, which was the only other place. Then Gillian stirred her drink and looked at the window and said, "We're doing that thing."

"What thing?"

"That thing where we run out of stuff. I can feel it coming, like a subway pulling in."

Eli's hand was already under the table, gripping his knee. He had planned to wait longer, to let the silence ripen, but the silence was not ripening, it was congealing. He let go of the knee. "Okay. I have an idea, and you're going to think I'm a weirdo."

"I already think you're a weirdo. You argued with Karimi for ten minutes about one point off."

"It was a matter of principle." He heard himself start to pontificate about rubrics and partial credit and the tyranny of the answer key, heard his voice climb into its lecturing register, and stopped. "Sorry. See, that's the problem. I do that. So the idea is, instead of that, we ask each other real questions. Hard ones. Trading off."

Gillian set down her spoon. "Like truth or dare without the dare."

"Sort of. There was this study." He laid it out carefully, the way he had rehearsed it, because he did not want to get it wrong: 1997, Arthur Aron, strangers paired up, taking turns asking each other thirty-six questions that got gradually more personal, and at the end those pairs felt closer than the pairs stuck with small talk. "So it's not just my scheme. It's science's scheme."

"It's a little insane," Gillian said. "I'm in."

They started easy, out of fairness, though Eli noticed the easy ones were not actually easy. What do you do when you can't sleep. What you would change about your senior year if you could. Gillian answered the second one without looking up from her cup: she would have quit orchestra in September instead of pretending until May that she was going to practice. He had sat behind her at the spring concert. She had played beautifully. He said so, and she said the girl next to her had been covering her part, and something subterranean shifted between them, a door opening onto a stairwell neither of them had known was there.

By the fourth question they were leaning across the table. By the ninth, Gillian had admitted she was scared of her roommate assignment at college, and Eli had admitted that he had chosen his school mostly because his mother cried when he first said the far one, and he had let the crying decide, and he did not know yet whether that was kindness or cowardice. "Both," Gillian said. "It can be both. That's not casuistry, that's just how things are."

"It might be casuistry. Letting yourself off easy with a nice word."

"Fine. Then it's both and you'll figure out which one it is more of later." She turned her cup a full circle on its saucer. "You're at, what, fourteen questions? You said thirty-six."

"We don't have to do all of them. The study did. But we're not the study."

"No," Gillian said. "We're ahead of the study. The study had strangers."

They got to twenty-three before the shop turned half its lights off, which was the barista's way of saying the evening had a deadline. Question twenty-three was Gillian's, and it arrived slowly, after a long sip: "What's the thing you want that you've never said out loud to anyone?"

Eli thought about the glovebox, the parked phone, the two readings and then a third. He had wanted the study to be a shortcut, a machine you could feed two people into, and it had turned out to be more like a map of a staircase that you still had to climb yourself, step by step, out loud, in order. Whether the closeness would last past tonight, past the parking lot, past September, the study could not tell him and neither could he. But that was tomorrow's question, and not one of the thirty-six.

He looked at her across the cold cups and said, "I want to be the kind of person who doesn't need a script. And I just used a script tonight."

Gillian reached over and stole the last corner of his muffin. "Twenty-four," she said. "Ask me anything."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: On a pyramid with five-year age groups, a bulge moves up one bar every five years, so today's large group of babies becomes a large group of schoolchildren soon after.
story:
Alexis had agreed to meet his mother at the travel agency at four, and he was twenty minutes early, so he sat in the moulded plastic chair by the window and took out his geography folder, because the presentation was due Thursday and he had promised Soleil he would have the argument settled by tonight. The assignment was to read a population pyramid and predict whether a country would need more schools or more nursing homes, and his pyramid, printed off in the school library at a angle so that the edges of the bars were blurred, showed a country with a fat base and a thinner stack above it. He had written in the margin, "More schools, obviously," and then crossed it out, because obviously was what got him a B on the last essay.

The agency smelled of carpet cleaner and old brochures. Behind the counter, a woman was sorting leaflets into a rack, and when the bell on the door had stopped its clatter she looked up and said, "You're not here for a package tour, I take it."

"Waiting for my mum," Alexis said. "She booked a trip. I'm doing homework." He held up the pyramid as evidence, the way you show a passport at a border.

Ms. Bautista came around the counter, wiping her hands on her skirt, and leaned over his folder. "Kenya," she read off the caption. "I sell safaris there. We keep these charts in the back for market work, you know. Where the young people are, that's where the bookings come from in ten years." She went to a filing cabinet and returned with a printed pyramid of her own, a different country, its shape narrowing almost to a point at the bottom and widening as it climbed. "Japan," she said. "Guess which one sells more cruises."

He looked at her chart and felt something shift, the way a word you've read wrong for years suddenly snaps into its right shape. His pyramid bulged at the bottom, in the zero to four bar, a wide shelf of babies. Her pyramid bulged higher up, in the middle. He had been thinking of the bulge as fixed, as if the babies would stay babies while everything around them aged, and that was the mistake. He counted the bars on the vertical axis, whispering the labels. "Zero to four, five to nine, ten to fourteen." Five-year age groups. "It moves up," he said.

"Moves up how?" Ms. Bautista pulled a chair over and sat, genuinely asking, as though he were the one with the filing cabinet full of charts.

"One bar every five years," Alexis said slowly, testing it as he said it. "The whole bulge. Today's large group of babies becomes a large group of schoolchildren soon after." He pulled his notebook toward him and wrote it down before the sentence could dissolve. The wide shelf at the bottom would, in five years, be sitting in the five to nine bar, and five years after that in the ten to fourteen bar, climbing like a wave through the stack. His phone buzzed on his knee. Soleil: "did you figure out when the boom hits the high school or are we presenting vibes." He typed back, "Working on it," and then, because it was true, "I had it wrong."

Soleil had argued in the library that they should predict nursing homes, because nursing homes were the future everywhere and it was the defensible answer, the answer that made them sound serious. Alexis had almost let himself be persuaded, half to avoid an argument and half because a conclusion that matched the general drift of the news felt safer than one that had to be defended with counting. He had even drafted a slide saying that. He found it now, folded behind the folder's back pocket, and read it with the particular discomfort of meeting your former self in the hallway. Maybe you couldn't absolve yourself of a lazy conclusion just by noticing it later, but you could at least stop repeating it.

"Can I borrow a pencil?" he asked. Ms. Bautista found him one, chewed at the end, and he didn't mind. On the back of a brochure for coastal resorts he drew the pyramid freehand, bars stacked like stairs, and marked the bulge with a cross. Then he drew an arrow straight up through the middle, one bar, then the next, then the next. The babies would reach secondary school age in roughly fifteen years, three bars of climbing, and if his own town's birth numbers were anything like the national ones, his old high school would feel the wave arrive just after he had finished university and, if he went into teaching as he sometimes thought he might, just as he arrived at the other end of a classroom.

The bell rang and his mother came in, talking already about departure dates and aisle seats, and Ms. Bautista stood up to serve her, the professional mask settling back over her face. But before she went she tapped the Japan chart with one finger and said, "The bulge climbs here too, you know. Same rule. It just ends somewhere else." Alexis looked at her pyramid again, at the wide middle bars that would rise into the grey heights of the chart, and understood that the counting answered a narrower question than he had wanted it to. Whether a country needed schools or nursing homes, which future to build for, that wasn't a thing a pyramid could decide. It could only tell you when.

He texted Soleil a photograph of the hand-drawn brochure, arrow climbing through the bars. "We were both half right," he wrote. "You want to redo the whole conclusion tonight?" The three dots appeared, vanished, appeared again, and behind them his mother was signing something and Ms. Bautista was sliding a ticket across the counter, and Alexis sat with the phone warm in his hand, waiting to find out which way they would go.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Early Action in US college admissions gives an early decision but is non-binding, so an admitted student may still choose not to enroll.
story:
The notice arrived on a Tuesday, folded into the mailbox between a grocery flyer and something from the dentist, and Jesse carried it to the public library unopened because the library was where he did his serious thinking. He had a table he liked, third floor, by the window overlooking the parking lot, close enough to the heating vent that his left hand stayed warm while his right froze, an imbalance he had come to regard as the natural condition of scholarship.

Sammy was already there, spread across two chairs with a laptop, a sandwich, and the general posture of someone who had been rejected by a college and wanted witnesses. "Deferred," Sammy said, before Jesse had even sat down. "Which means they're keeping me in a little jar labeled maybe. I'm plankton, Jesse. I'm zooplankton."

"Could be worse." Jesse set the envelope on the table, address side down, and looked at it the way you look at a dog that might or might not be friendly. The envelope was thin. Everyone knew a thin envelope meant no, except sometimes it didn't, which was one of the many ways this process resembled a religion: lots of lore, no reliable prophecy.

"You're not opening it?"

"I'm letting it acclimate." He slid it toward the vent. "Also my hands are cold."

Sammy leaned over and read the return address, and something in Sammy's face catalyzed the whole thing, because Jesse had applied Early Action without fully understanding what he'd done, had checked a box back in October mainly because Braeden had checked it, and Braeden's mother had called it strategic. It had felt strategic at the time, like moving a rook. Now the rook had possibly come back with news.

He opened it. The letter inside said, in the university's most munificent font, that he was admitted, class of whatever, congratulations, and Jesse read it three times and then laughed, once, in a way that startled a man at the next table into protecting his crossword.

"Okay," Sammy said. "Okay. That's the jar. You're out of the jar. You're a free man."

"I mean, kind of."

"What do you mean kind of, it says admitted, it says congratulations, it has a seal on it, look at the seal. That seal cost more than my laptop."

Jesse turned the letter over, looking for the catch, because there had to be a catch, because his father had warned him about catches, though his father had gone to a state school in 1989 and his knowledge of admissions was mostly folklore. "It's Early Action," Jesse said slowly, and then, because Sammy was already opening his mouth, "which means it's not binding. I got in early, but I don't have to go."

Sammy blinked. "That's a thing? You can just get in and then not go?"

"Early Action gives you the decision early, and it's non-binding, so an admitted student can still choose not to enroll." He had read that somewhere, back in October, in a paragraph he'd skimmed on his phone while eating cereal. It had seemed like fine print then. Now it felt like the whole point. He could say yes to this school in December and still, in the spring, hold every other offer in his hands and pick. He could keep applying. He could stop. Nobody was going to make him do anything, which was either freedom or a trap, depending on the hour.

"That's a munificent system," Sammy said, testing the word. "Generous, I mean. Wait, that's not the point. The point is you got in. Are you going or not?"

"I don't know. That's the actual point. I hadn't thought past the envelope." He looked out the window at the parking lot, where a woman was trying to parallel park a van with the patience of a saint and the accuracy of a drunk. Somewhere in his backpack were four half-finished applications, four essays about challenge and growth, and he had been planning to finish them over winter break with the joy of dental surgery. If he stopped now, December would be soft and sweet and application-free. If he kept going, he kept his options, and options, his economics teacher liked to say, have value, though she'd never said how you paid for them, or in what currency.

Ms. Li, the librarian whose domain was the third floor and who had a habit of materializing when people whispered too long, stopped at their table with a cart of returns. "Someone got good news," she said. It wasn't a question; Sammy's face had apparently been broadcasting.

"Jesse got into college," Sammy said. "And now he's being weird about it."

"I'm not being weird. I'm deliberating."

"You're letting a good letter get cold next to a vent."

Ms. Li smiled at that, picked up the crossword man's abandoned newspaper, and rolled her cart onward. Jesse folded the letter and put it in his pocket, where he could feel it against his leg like a receipt for something he hadn't decided to buy yet. He pulled his laptop toward him and opened the file with the four unfinished essays, cursor blinking in the middle of a sentence about his grandfather, which was as far as inspiration had carried him in November.

"So?" Sammy said.

"So I'm going to finish them. All four. The acceptance is real, but it's one door, not the house." He typed a clause, deleted it, typed it again. "Or I'm going to sit here till closing and decide nothing. It could go either way, honestly."

"You're describing my whole life," Sammy said, and stole a quarter of the sandwich back.
